meta.sourceSection: Table 2A-1, sign shapes; Section 2B.04, STOP signs.
meta.note: The MUTCD states when an agency installs a STOP sign, never what a rider must do, so the answer is the converse of an installation warrant rather than a statement in the document.

content.question: You are riding up to an intersection and see this sign. Nothing is coming from either direction. What does the sign tell you to do?

media.alt: A red eight-sided road sign with a white border and white letters reading STOP.

choices.text: Come to a complete stop before entering the intersection
Slow to walking pace and roll through, since the way is clear
Stop only if a stop line is painted on the pavement
Stop only when another vehicle or a pedestrian is approaching

content.explanation: The octagon is reserved for one sign in the national standard, and that sign goes up only where a full stop is always required.

guide.text: A stop sign always calls for a full stop, even when no one else is coming.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, under The Right Motorcycle For You.

content.question: You are choosing your first motorcycle. Which of these tells you the bike is the right size for you?

choices.text: Your feet reach the ground while you are seated on it
The engine is large enough to keep up with highway traffic
It is heavy enough to feel steady when you come to a stop
The seat is high enough to see over the roofs of cars

content.explanation: A motorcycle fits you when your feet reach the ground while you sit on it.

guide.label: Right size bike
guide.text: Your feet reach the ground from the seat.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Helmet Selection.

content.question: What happens to a helmet that is resting on your head but not strapped on, if you crash?

choices.text: It can come off before it has protected your head
It stays put, because your head is pressed up into it
It protects your head but is far more likely to crack
It shifts back and protects your neck instead of your skull

content.explanation: A helmet only works while it is on your head, so the strap goes on every time you ride. Left unfastened, it can leave your head in a crash before it has absorbed anything.

guide.text: A helmet that is not strapped on can come off in a crash before it protects you.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Eye and Face Protection.

content.question: You are deciding between goggles and a face shield. How do the two differ in what they protect?

choices.text: A face shield covers the whole face; goggles protect only the eyes
Goggles cover the whole face; a face shield protects only the eyes
Both protect the eyes only, but a face shield also cuts wind noise
Both cover the whole face, but goggles seal better against dust

content.explanation: A face shield protects the whole face in a crash. Goggles guard the eyes and leave the rest of the face exposed.

guide.label: Face shield
guide.text: Covers the whole face. Goggles guard the eyes only.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Eye and Face Protection.
meta.note: The manuals explain no mechanism for a windshield not being eye protection, so neither does the explanation. Florida counts glasses as eye protection, so the question claims only that they let the wind in, as Florida also says.

content.question: Your motorcycle is fitted with a large windshield. What eye protection do you still need?

choices.text: A face shield or goggles; a windshield will not keep wind from your eyes
Nothing more, since the windshield already does a face shield's job
Glasses, which are enough once a windshield blocks most of the wind
Nothing more, provided you keep to lower speeds and shorter trips

content.explanation: A windshield, however large, does not stop wind reaching your eyes, so you still need a face shield or goggles. Glasses fall short too. Your eyes can still water behind them, and turning your head into the wind can pull them off.

guide.text: A windshield does not protect your eyes. Wear a face shield or goggles, since glasses alone let the wind in.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Eye and Face Protection.

content.question: You will be riding home after dark. What does that mean for a tinted face shield or tinted goggles?

choices.text: Change to clear protection, which is what low light calls for
Keep them on; the tint cuts headlight glare from oncoming traffic
Keep them on, since any eye protection beats none after dark
Lift them clear of your eyes and ride without eye protection

content.explanation: Tinted eye protection is for daylight only. Don't wear it when there is little light, such as after dark.

guide.label: Tinted shield or goggles
guide.text: Daylight only. Change to clear before riding at night or in low light.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Clothing.
meta.note: No held document explains why covered skin dehydrates less, so the explanation states no mechanism.

content.question: It is a hot summer day. Besides crash protection, what does a riding jacket do for you?

choices.text: It helps keep you from becoming dehydrated on the ride
Nothing on a hot day; its only other job is keeping you warm
It makes the wind easier to feel, so you can judge your speed
It cuts down the engine noise that reaches your ears

content.explanation: Keep your jacket on when it is hot. Covering up helps head off dehydration, and many jackets are made for warm weather, so you can stay protected and still be comfortable.

guide.text: A jacket helps head off dehydration, so wear one on hot days as well.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, in the protective gear list.

content.question: A rider avoids earplugs because they think it will stop them hearing traffic. What does hearing protection actually do?

choices.text: Brings the noise level down while still letting horns and sirens through
Blocks outside sound completely, which is why it suits track use only
Adds nothing under a full face helmet, which already blocks the noise
Guards your hearing only above highway speeds, so it is optional in town

content.explanation: Hearing protection brings the overall noise level down without shutting out horns and sirens. Over time, wind noise alone can damage your hearing.

guide.label: Hearing protection
guide.text: Cuts wind noise without shutting out horns and sirens.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, under Get Familiar with the Controls.
meta.note: CA's list says headlight dimmer switch where the MOM says headlight switch, so the stem asks about the headlight switch generally.

content.question: Before taking an unfamiliar motorcycle into traffic, which controls should you be able to reach and work without hunting for them?

choices.text: The turn signals, horn, headlight switch and engine cut-off switch
The turn signals and horn only, as the rest are used at a standstill
The brakes and clutch only, as those are the controls that vary least
No particular ones; familiarity comes from riding it a few miles

content.explanation: On a motorcycle you have not ridden before, find the turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel valve and engine cut-off switch first, then work each one until you can do it without looking.

guide.text: On an unfamiliar bike, learn the signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel valve and cut-off switch by feel before riding.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking.

content.question: You are slowing for a red light in no particular hurry. Which brakes should you use?

choices.text: Both of them, the same as you would for a sudden stop
The rear only, keeping the front in reserve for emergencies
The front only, since it does most of the stopping
Either one on its own, as long as you leave enough room

content.explanation: Use both brakes every time you slow or stop. Ordinary stops are where the habit gets built, so that reaching for both is automatic when a stop has to happen fast.

guide.text: Use both brakes every time you slow or stop, not only in emergencies.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking.
meta.note: CA states three-quarters where the other manuals state 70% or more, so the question asks for the floor all four support.

content.question: How much of a motorcycle's total stopping power comes from the front brake?

choices.text: 70 percent or more
Roughly 50 percent
Under 30 percent
It depends on the motorcycle

content.explanation: The front brake supplies at least 70 percent of a motorcycle's stopping power. It is the more powerful of the two, and it is safe to use when it is used properly.

guide.label: Front brake
guide.text: At least 70% of total stopping power.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking.

content.question: What is the right way to apply the front brake lever?

choices.text: Squeeze it smoothly, building pressure as the motorcycle slows
Grab it quickly so the brake takes hold right away
Pump it on and off to keep the front wheel turning
Apply it hard at first, then ease off as the motorcycle slows

content.explanation: Squeeze the front brake lever smoothly and build pressure as you slow. Grabbing it or applying sudden pressure can lock the front wheel and cost you control.

guide.text: Squeeze the front brake smoothly and build pressure. Never grab it.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking in a Corner.

content.question: You are leaned over in a curve and need to stop quickly. The road ahead of you is clear. What should you do first?

choices.text: Bring the motorcycle upright first, then apply the brakes
Brake as hard as you would in a straight line, then straighten up
Lean further to tighten your line, then brake once the curve opens
Use the rear brake on its own until the curve has ended

content.explanation: Grip spent on leaning is grip you can't spend on stopping. With a clear road, straighten up first so the tires can take full braking. If the road won't allow it, brake gently while leaned and add pressure as you come upright.

guide.text: In a curve with room to spare, stand the motorcycle up before you brake hard.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Turning.

content.question: A rider enters a curve faster than they can hold. What are the usual results?

choices.text: Crossing into another lane, leaving the road, or skidding from hard braking
The tires grip harder at speed, so the line holds
The rear tire losing grip because of a sudden loss of air pressure
The engine losing power and the machine settling onto its side

content.explanation: Too much speed into a curve is a common mistake, and it ends one of two ways: the motorcycle runs wide, into the next lane or off the road, or the rider grabs the brakes and skids.

guide.text: Take a curve too fast and you run wide or panic on the brakes and skid. Slow down before it.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Turning.

content.question: As you ride through a curve, where should you be looking, and how?

choices.text: Through the curve to where you want to end up, turning your head only
Through the curve, turning your head and shoulders together to face it
At the pavement just ahead of your front wheel, to catch surface hazards
At the edge line beside you, to judge how close you are to the shoulder

content.explanation: Aim your eyes at the exit of the curve, the place you mean to end up. Move only your head to do it, leaving your shoulders square, and hold your eyes level instead of letting them tilt with the motorcycle.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Turning.

content.question: You are riding at road speed and need to turn left. What makes the motorcycle lean into the turn?

choices.text: Pressing forward on the left handgrip
Pulling back on the left handgrip
Pressing forward on the right handgrip
Putting your weight on the left footrest

content.explanation: At road speed a motorcycle has to lean before it will turn, and pressure on a handgrip is what tips it. Push forward on the grip on the side you want to go: the left grip for a left turn, the right grip for a right.

guide.text: To turn at speed, push forward on the grip on the side you're turning toward.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Turning.

content.question: What decides how far a motorcycle has to lean in a turn?

choices.text: How fast you are going and how sharp the turn is
How heavy the motorcycle is and how it is loaded
How much tread depth the tires have left on them
Which gear the motorcycle happens to be in at the time

content.explanation: Lean angle rises with speed and with how tight the turn is, so a fast or sharp turn takes more lean than a slow, gentle one.

guide.label: Lean angle
guide.text: Rises with speed and with how sharp the turn is.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Turning.

content.question: In a normal turn taken at road speed, how should your body sit in relation to the motorcycle?

choices.text: Leaning with the motorcycle, at the same angle it does
Upright, while the motorcycle leans underneath you
Leaning further into the turn than the motorcycle does
Leaning away from the turn to work against the lean

content.explanation: In a normal turn the rider leans with the motorcycle, both at the same angle. Slow, tight turns are the exception and call for something different.

guide.text: Through a normal turn, you and the motorcycle tilt by the same amount.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Turning.

content.question: You are making a slow, tight turn, such as a U-turn in a parking lot. How should your body sit in relation to the motorcycle?

choices.text: Upright, while the motorcycle leans underneath you
Leaning with the motorcycle, at the same angle it does
Leaning further into the turn than the motorcycle does
Leaning back to take weight off the front wheel

content.explanation: In a slow, tight turn, keep your body upright and let the motorcycle lean underneath you. That is the opposite of a normal turn, where rider and machine lean together.

guide.text: In a slow, tight turn, only the motorcycle leans; your body stays vertical.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Body Position.

content.question: How should your right wrist be positioned when you take hold of the throttle?

choices.text: Flat, so you don't open the throttle by accident
Angled down, so you can roll on faster when you need to
Angled up, so your fingers stay clear of the brake lever
However it falls, since grip pressure is what matters

content.explanation: Take hold of the right grip with the back of your wrist level. A wrist that starts out bent makes it easy to give more throttle than you meant to.

guide.text: Hold the throttle with your right wrist flat, to avoid adding throttle by accident.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Body Position.
meta.note: GA states the knee position without the balance-through-turns reason the other three give, so the question asks the position only.

content.question: Where should your knees be while the motorcycle is moving?

choices.text: Against the gas tank
Spread wide of the tank, to steady the machine
Clear of the tank, so you can shift your weight freely
Loose and away from the machine, to soak up bumps

content.explanation: Keep your knees against the gas tank while the motorcycle is moving.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Body Position.

content.question: Where should your feet be while riding, and what should you avoid doing with them?

choices.text: Firmly on the footrests, with your toes not pointing down
Firmly on the footrests, with your toes pointed down for grip
Resting lightly on the footrests, ready to put a foot down
Hanging below the footrests, ready to feel the road surface

content.explanation: Plant your feet on the footrests and leave them there. Toes angled down can snag on the road surface and get trapped under the footrest.

guide.text: Feet firm on the footrests, toes never pointing down.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking.

content.question: What can happen if you grab the front brake or stamp down on the rear?

choices.text: A wheel can lock and you can lose control
The brakes fade and give you nothing for a few seconds
The motorcycle stops shorter than with smooth pressure
Nothing much, as long as you are going in a straight line

content.explanation: Grabbing the front brake or jamming the rear can lock a wheel, and a locked wheel costs you control. Squeeze the front and press the rear instead.

guide.text: Grabbing the front brake or jamming the rear can lock a wheel and cost you control.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Turning.

content.question: What should you be doing with the throttle as you ride through a turn?

choices.text: Easing it on, to keep speed steady or build it a little
Closing it fully, and coasting until the turn opens up
Rolling off steadily, so speed drops through the turn
Holding it exactly where it was before you entered

content.explanation: Feed in a little throttle through the turn, enough to keep your speed steady or let it build gently. Steady drive through the turn is what keeps the motorcycle settled.

guide.text: Through a turn, ease the throttle on to keep your speed steady or build it a little. It steadies the motorcycle.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: How do you change up and down through a motorcycle's gears?

choices.text: Lift the shift lever to go up, press it down to go down
Press the shift lever down to go up, lift it to go down
Lift the lever for every change; the clutch picks direction
Twist the lever forward to go up and backward to go down

content.explanation: Lift the shift lever to change up a gear and press it down to change down. Each lift or press moves one gear.

guide.text: Lift the gearshift lever to change up a gear and press it down to change down, one gear each time.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: On a typical motorcycle gear pattern, where does neutral sit?

choices.text: Between first and second gear
Below first gear, at the bottom of the pattern
Above the highest gear, at the top of the pattern
Nowhere fixed; the position changes with the machine

content.explanation: Neutral sits between first and second gear, so getting to it takes a partial shift: a light lift from first, or a light press down from second. Above second, the gears run on in order.

guide.label: Typical gear pattern
guide.text: 1-N-2-3-4-5+, with neutral between first and second.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking.

content.question: How are a motorcycle's brakes controlled?

choices.text: Two separate controls, one for each wheel
One control that works both wheels together
One control for both wheels, plus a parking brake
Two controls that both act on the front wheel

content.explanation: On most motorcycles each wheel has its own brake control, worked separately: a hand lever for the front and a foot pedal for the rear.

guide.text: Two brake controls: a front hand lever and a rear foot pedal.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking.

content.question: The motorcycle is upright and traveling in a straight line. What gives you the shortest stop?

choices.text: Both brakes applied fully, without locking either wheel
The front brake applied fully on its own
Both brakes applied until the rear wheel locks
The rear brake applied fully, with the front used lightly

content.explanation: The shortest straight-line stop comes from applying both brakes fully without letting either wheel lock.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking.

content.question: What should you be doing with your knees and your eyes while braking hard?

choices.text: Knees against the tank, eyes up and looking well ahead
Knees out wide, eyes down on the front wheel
Knees against the tank, eyes down on the instruments
Knees out wide, eyes fixed on the vehicle ahead

content.explanation: Grip the tank with your knees and keep your gaze up and far ahead. Holding that posture helps the motorcycle stop in a straight line.

guide.text: Braking hard, press your knees to the tank and look far ahead; it keeps the stop straight.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking.

content.question: A rider avoids the front brake, worried it will pitch them over the handlebars. What is true?

choices.text: Used properly, it is safe
The worry is sound, so it belongs below walking pace only
The worry is sound on anything but a dry, level surface
It is safe only on a motorcycle fitted with anti-lock brakes

content.explanation: Used properly, the front brake is perfectly safe, and avoiding it throws away most of your stopping power.

guide.text: Used correctly, the front brake is safe, and it does most of your stopping.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking.

content.question: What happens to front wheel traction once you start braking, and what does that allow?

choices.text: Traction rises as weight shifts forward, so the front brake can be squeezed harder
Traction drops as weight shifts forward, so the front brake must be eased off
Traction stays where it was, so front brake pressure should stay constant
Traction moves to the rear, so the rear brake should take over the stop

content.explanation: Braking shifts the motorcycle's weight forward, which puts more traction at the front wheel. That is why front brake pressure can build after the stop has begun.

guide.text: Braking shifts weight forward and adds front traction, so front brake pressure can build as you slow.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking in a Corner.

content.question: How does lean angle affect the traction available for braking?

choices.text: The further it is leaned, the less traction is left for braking
The further it is leaned, the more traction is left for braking
Lean angle changes cornering grip but not braking grip
Lean angle matters only on a wet or loose surface

content.explanation: A leaned motorcycle has less traction left for braking. As it straightens up, traction comes back and you can brake harder.

guide.text: The further a motorcycle is leaned, the less traction is left for braking.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Linked and Integrated Braking Systems.

content.question: On a motorcycle with a linked braking system, what happens when you use one brake control?

choices.text: Both brakes are applied
Only the control you used is applied
The front brake is disabled while the rear is in use
The system picks one brake based on your speed

content.explanation: Linked brakes tie the front and rear together, so either the lever or the pedal brakes both wheels. Integrated brakes are a related setup: pressing the rear pedal also brings in some front brake. Your owner's manual explains how yours behaves.

guide.label: Linked braking
guide.text: Lever or pedal, either one brakes both wheels. An integrated system adds some front brake when you use the rear.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Anti-Lock Braking Systems.

content.question: What does an anti-lock braking system do, and when does it act?

choices.text: Keeps the wheels from locking when you brake too hard
Shortens every stop, whether or not a wheel is about to lock
Releases the brakes entirely once a wheel locks, until you reapply
Works on the front wheel only, where lock-up is most dangerous

content.explanation: ABS steps in when you press a brake hard enough to lock its wheel. It eases the pressure off and back on, over and over, so the wheel keeps turning and you can keep braking hard without a skid.

guide.text: ABS keeps a wheel from locking when you brake too hard, so a panic stop doesn't turn into a skid.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Anti-Lock Braking Systems.

content.question: How quickly can an anti-lock braking system release and reapply brake pressure?

choices.text: More than 15 times a second
About eight times a second
About four times a second
It does not cycle; it simply caps how much pressure reaches the brake

content.explanation: The system can ease off and reapply the brakes more than 15 times every second.

guide.label: ABS cycle rate
guide.text: More than 15 times a second.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Body Position.

content.question: How should you position yourself on the seat?

choices.text: So your arms are free to steer the motorcycle
As far back as the seat allows, for a relaxed reach to the bars
Leaning forward over the tank, to keep weight off the rear wheel
Leaning your weight on the bars, arms locked straight

content.explanation: Sit so your arms are free to steer the motorcycle.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: When should you shift down through the gears?

choices.text: While slowing or stopping, and to get more power for accelerating
Only when coming to a complete stop
Only when you want extra power to speed up
Only once the engine begins to lug at low revs

content.explanation: Downshift on the way to a stop, a gear at a time as your speed falls. Dropping a gear is also how you get extra pull when you need to accelerate.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: What happens if you shift into a lower gear while still traveling too fast for it?

choices.text: A jolt, and possibly a skidding rear wheel
The engine stalls and the motorcycle coasts to a stop
The transmission refuses the shift until you slow down
Nothing, as long as you release the clutch smoothly

content.explanation: A gear too low for your speed jerks the motorcycle and can break the rear tire loose. Let your speed come down far enough before you select it.

guide.text: Downshift only once you've slowed enough, or the motorcycle can jolt and skid its rear wheel.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: What effect does shifting to a lower gear have on your speed?

choices.text: It slows you down, a bit like braking
It speeds the motorcycle up until you close the throttle
It raises engine revs but leaves road speed unchanged
It slows the motorcycle only when you are on a downhill grade

content.explanation: A lower gear has the engine hold the motorcycle back and slows it, an effect known as engine braking.

guide.text: Downshifting slows the motorcycle on its own. This is engine braking.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Body Position.

content.question: What tells you that you are sitting at the right distance from the handlebars?

choices.text: A slight bend in your arms as you hold the grips
Your arms are straight and fully extended at the grips
Your chest almost touches the tank when you reach the grips
Your elbows are locked, with your shoulders doing the work

content.explanation: Move up the seat until your elbows keep a slight bend with your hands on the grips. That bend lets you push on the bars to steer without leaning out to reach them.

guide.text: Sit close enough to the bars that your elbows stay slightly bent.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Body Position.

content.question: Where should the handlebars put your hands in relation to your elbows?

choices.text: No higher than your elbows
Well above your elbows, for leverage on the bars
Level with your shoulders, whatever that does to your elbows
Wherever the bars came set from the factory

content.explanation: Adjust the bars until your hands sit level with your elbows or a little lower. Hands at that height put your arms in the position to steer well.

guide.text: Set the bars at a height that keeps your hands at or below your elbows.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: Where is a motorcycle's gearshift lever, and which foot operates it?

choices.text: In front of the left footrest, worked by the left foot
In front of the right footrest, worked by the right foot
Behind the left footrest, worked by the left heel
On the handlebar, worked by the left hand

content.explanation: You change gears with your left foot, using the lever just ahead of the left footrest.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: How many gears does a typical motorcycle have?

choices.text: Five, with some having four or six
Four, with some having three or five
Six, with some having five or seven
Three, with some having two or four

content.explanation: Five is the usual number of gears, though some motorcycles have four and others six.

guide.label: Gear count
guide.text: Five on most motorcycles, with some at four or six.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: When should you shift up to a higher gear?

choices.text: Before the revs climb too high, but not so early the engine labors
As soon as the motorcycle begins to move in each gear
Only once the engine reaches its maximum recommended speed
Whenever the engine note drops, whatever the road speed

content.explanation: Change up while the engine still has room below its top revs. Shifting too early is the opposite mistake, and leaves the engine laboring at low speed.

guide.text: Change up before the engine nears its rev limit, but not so early that it labors.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: When might you need the brakes to slow down before a downshift is safe?

choices.text: Going downhill, or when the next gear is first
Riding uphill, or shifting into top gear
On any downshift, since engine braking is never enough
Only on a wet surface, where the rear can break loose

content.explanation: Going downhill, or when the next gear down is first, you may have to brake to get your speed low enough for the gear. Slow first, then shift.

guide.text: Downhill or before shifting into first, use the brakes to get your speed down before the downshift.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: Which gear should you be in while stopped in traffic?

choices.text: First, ready to pull away fast if you have to
Neutral, so your clutch hand can rest
Second, so that pulling away is smoother
Whichever gear you happened to be in when you stopped

content.explanation: Wait at a stop in first gear. If you suddenly need to get out of the way, you're ready to go.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Shifting Gears.

content.question: When should you change gear in relation to a turn?

choices.text: Before entering it, and smoothly if you must shift mid-turn
Mid-turn, where the lean settles the machine
After exiting it, once the motorcycle is upright again
It makes no difference where in the turn you shift

content.explanation: Get into the right gear before the turn begins. If you do have to change gear partway through, make the change gently, since a sudden surge of power at the rear tire can make it slide.

guide.text: Pick your gear before a turn, and make any mid-turn shift a gentle one.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Braking.

content.question: How should rear brake pressure change as you brake hard?

choices.text: Light, then lighter still, as weight shifts off the rear
Light, then heavier, as the motorcycle slows down
Steady throughout, matching what the front brake is doing
Heavy at first, then released once the front takes over

content.explanation: Use light and then lighter pressure on the rear brake as you slow. Weight shifting forward leaves less traction at the rear, so heavy rear pressure can skid the wheel.

guide.text: Rear brake pressure goes light, then lighter, as weight shifts forward.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Keeping Your Distance.

content.question: What does a cushion of space around your motorcycle give you if another road user makes a mistake?

choices.text: Time to react, and room to steer or stop
A shorter stopping distance at any speed
The right of way over nearby vehicles
Room to ride faster than the traffic around you

content.explanation: Space around the motorcycle buys you time to react and room to steer or stop when someone else makes a mistake.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Lane Positions.

content.question: Vehicles are traveling in the lanes on both sides of you. Where in your own lane is usually the best place to ride?

media.alt: Top-down view of three lanes of traffic heading the same way. The middle lane is marked into three equal strips. A car travels in the lane on its left and a truck in the lane on its right.

choices.text: In the center of the lane
In the left third, where most riders sit by default
In the right third, away from faster traffic
In whichever third is farthest from the larger vehicle

content.explanation: Think of the lane as having a left, middle and right third. Move away from whichever side the trouble is on, and with traffic on both sides, the middle third is usually the place to be.

guide.text: Move to the side of your lane away from a hazard. With traffic on both sides, the middle is usually best.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Lane Positions.

content.question: What should your choice of position within the lane help you do?

choices.text: Stay out of other drivers' blind spots
Keep one steady position so drivers can predict you
Leave room beside you for faster traffic to squeeze past
Stay close enough to the vehicle ahead that nobody cuts in

content.explanation: A good lane position does several jobs. It keeps you visible and gives you a clear view, keeps you out of blind spots and away from other vehicles' wind blast, signals what you plan to do and leaves you a way out. As traffic shifts, so should your position.

guide.text: A lane position should keep you seen and seeing, out of blind spots and wind blast, with a way out.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Lane Positions.

content.question: On a dry road, can you ride in the center of your lane?

choices.text: Yes, it is as usable as any other part
Yes, if you ride on top of any discoloration
No, oil dripped by cars makes it too slick
No, it hides you from the drivers ahead

content.explanation: Yes. Cars drip oil along a narrow band down the middle of the lane, but on dry pavement that band still gives enough grip, and you can also ride just beside it and stay central. Rain is what makes it slick.

guide.text: On dry pavement, the center of the lane is as usable as anywhere else in it.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Vehicles Alongside.

content.question: You are riding right beside a car in the next lane. What should you do?

media.alt: Top-down view of two lanes heading the same way. A motorcycle rides level with the rear door of a car in the lane beside it.

choices.text: Change your speed until you are no longer beside it
Match its speed so its driver can keep track of you
Tap your brake light so its driver knows you are there
Stay put, since drivers check the next lane before moving over

content.explanation: Riding alongside a car puts you where its driver may not see you, so it could change lanes into you, and it also boxes you in if something goes wrong ahead. Get ahead of it or fall back until no one is beside you.

guide.text: Don't ride alongside cars in the next lane: get ahead or fall back until you have open space on both sides.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Following Another Vehicle.

content.question: How do you check your following distance?

choices.text: Time the gap in seconds against a fixed point on the road
Estimate how many car lengths separate you from the vehicle ahead
Judge the gap by how large the vehicle ahead looks
Watch how quickly the gap closes each time the vehicle ahead brakes

content.explanation: Following distance is measured in seconds. Pick something fixed on or beside the road ahead, begin counting as the back of the vehicle in front passes it, and stop when you get there.

guide.text: Count following distance in seconds, from when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point until you reach it.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Following Another Vehicle.

content.question: When should you leave more than your usual following distance?

choices.text: When you cannot see past the vehicle ahead
When traffic is light and spread out
When the pavement is dry and clean
When you are riding a road you know well

content.explanation: Add to your gap whenever stopping might take longer or trouble could come with less warning: on a slick surface, behind a vehicle you can't see around, in dense traffic, or when your motorcycle needs extra distance to stop.

guide.text: Give yourself a bigger gap on slick roads, in dense traffic and behind anything you can't see around.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Following Another Vehicle.

content.question: In traffic, how much distance does a motorcycle need to stop, compared with a car?

choices.text: About the same as a car
About half as much, since it is lighter
Twice as much, since it has only two tires
Less, as long as both brakes are used

content.explanation: A motorcycle stops in about the same distance as a car, so it needs just as much room ahead in traffic. Riding too close to the vehicle ahead contributes to motorcycle crashes.

guide.label: A motorcycle's stopping distance
guide.text: About the same as a car's.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Following Another Vehicle.

content.question: You have stopped behind another vehicle. Why leave a good gap in front of you?

choices.text: To leave room to move if a driver behind is not slowing down
Because the vehicle ahead may roll forward without warning
So other drivers cannot squeeze in front of you
So you can pull away before the vehicle ahead does

content.explanation: At a stop, the gap in front is your way out. If a car behind is coming too fast to stop, you can pull forward or to the side, and if the vehicle ahead rolls back, it won't reach you.

guide.text: Stop with room in front of you, so you can move if a car behind isn't stopping.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Following Another Vehicle.

content.question: You are following a car. Where in your lane are you most likely to be seen by its driver?

choices.text: The center, in view of the inside rearview mirror
The far left, in view of the driver's side mirror
The far right, clear of the driver's blind spot
Anywhere, since drivers check every mirror equally

content.explanation: Drivers check the mirror inside the car far more often than the side mirrors. Riding the middle of the lane puts you in that inside mirror; toward either edge, you may show up only in a side mirror.

guide.text: Behind a car, ride the middle of the lane, where you show up in its inside rearview mirror.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Being Followed.

content.question: A driver is following you too closely. What is the best way to deal with it?

choices.text: Let them by, or slow down and open more space ahead
Speed up until they drop back in your mirror
Brake sharply once so they get the message and back off
Close up on the vehicle ahead so they can't pass

content.explanation: Getting a tailgater in front of you solves the problem, so let them by when you can. When you can't, ease off and widen the gap ahead: you both then have room to stop, and the driver is more likely to go around. Speeding up just moves the same problem to a higher speed.

guide.text: Let a tailgater by, or ease off and widen the gap ahead. Speeding up only gets you a faster tailgater.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Lane Positions.

content.question: Where are you most likely to find big buildups of oil and grease on the road?

choices.text: At busy intersections and toll booths
On bridges and overpasses
Along the shoulder, where cars pull off
On long, straight stretches of highway

content.explanation: Oil and grease collect most heavily at busy intersections and toll booths. Keep your tires off those patches.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Passing.

content.question: Before you pull out to pass a car, where in your lane should you be?

choices.text: Toward the left side, keeping a safe gap behind it
Close behind its bumper, ready to accelerate
The right portion, close up to pass quickly
The center, where its driver can see you in the mirror

content.explanation: Hang back at a normal following distance and move to the left side of your lane. From there you can see past the car, and other drivers can see you. Then signal, look ahead for oncoming traffic, and check your mirrors and blind spot.

guide.text: Set up a pass from the left side of your lane, a safe gap behind the car, and signal and check before pulling out.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Passing.

content.question: While you are passing another vehicle, what should you avoid?

choices.text: Lingering in its blind spot
Speeding up once you are in the passing lane
Checking your mirrors before moving back
Signaling again before you return to your lane

content.explanation: Once you move out to pass, speed up and get through the other driver's blind spot without lingering. Before moving back, signal and check your mirrors and over your shoulder, then cancel the signal once you are back in your lane.

guide.text: When passing, get through the other driver's blind spot without lingering, then signal and check before moving back.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Being Passed.

content.question: A car is passing you from behind. Where in your lane should you ride?

choices.text: In the middle of your lane
Close to the passing car, so its driver can see you
On the lane line nearest the car, to hold your space
Wherever you happen to be, since it must go around you

content.explanation: Holding the middle of your lane keeps a margin between you and the passing car. Close to it, one small steering error by either of you could mean a sideswipe, and a mirror or something tossed from a window can reach you.

guide.text: Keep to the middle of your lane while a car passes, clear of its mirrors and of anything tossed from it.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Lane Sharing.

content.question: On a dry road, where in your lane should you ride to discourage drivers from squeezing past you in it?

choices.text: In the middle of your lane
Near the edge of the lane, to give them room to get by
Close behind the vehicle ahead, so there is no gap to fill
On the lane line, where you are easiest to see

content.explanation: A rider near either edge of the lane leaves a gap that tempts a driver to share it. Holding the middle takes that gap away. Two vehicles side by side in one lane leave each other no room for a sudden move.

guide.text: Hold the middle of your lane on a dry road, and drivers have no gap to squeeze into beside you.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Lane Sharing.

content.question: When are drivers most tempted to squeeze past a motorcycle within its own lane?

choices.text: As you slow to turn at an intersection
When traffic is light and moving freely
When you are riding in the center of your lane
On a stretch of highway far from any exit

content.explanation: Watch for it whenever a driver sees a gap: as you slow to turn at an intersection or head for an exit, in packed stop-and-go traffic, and when the driver simply wants to get past you.

guide.text: Expect drivers to try squeezing past in your lane as you slow for a turn or exit, in packed traffic, and when they want to pass.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Merging Vehicles.

content.question: A car is merging onto the highway from an entrance ramp beside you, and the lane to your other side is full. What should you do?

choices.text: Speed up or slow down to make a gap for it
Hold your speed, since its driver will see you and fit in
Sound the horn and keep going at the same speed
Pull onto the left shoulder to let it in

content.explanation: Assume a driver coming down the ramp may not have spotted you. The easy answer is a lane change; with that lane full, change your speed instead so the car has somewhere to go.

guide.text: Make room for merging drivers: move over a lane, or change your speed when you can't.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Being Passed.
meta.note: FL puts the rider in the farthest portion, TX and CA in the middle, so the answer asks only what all three support: away from the side nearest the passing vehicle.

content.question: A large truck is passing you. Where in your lane gives you more room for error if its wind blast hits?

choices.text: Away from the side of the lane nearest the truck
Close to the truck, where it shelters you from the wind
On the lane line next to it, so its driver can see you
It makes no difference, since the blast is over in a moment

content.explanation: Wind from a passing truck or other large vehicle can push the motorcycle and affect your control. Keeping away from the side of your lane nearest it gives you more room for error.

guide.text: When a large vehicle passes, keep away from the side of your lane nearest it. Its wind blast can push you.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Search.

content.question: As you ride toward an intersection, what should you be searching for besides hazards?

choices.text: An escape path you could move into if you had to
A driver who seems ready to wave you through
The quickest gap for getting ahead of traffic
Nothing more, until something actually goes wrong

content.explanation: Look for escape paths as well as hazards, and pick them out before you need one. At an intersection, that means knowing where you could go if a vehicle turns or pulls into your way.

guide.text: Search for escape paths as well as hazards before anything goes wrong.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Search.

content.question: About how far ahead should you search, to spot trouble early enough to plan for it?

media.alt: Top-down view of a motorcycle in its lane, with a short shaded band just ahead of it and a second band much farther up the road.

choices.text: About 12 seconds
About 2 seconds
About 4 seconds
About 30 seconds

content.explanation: Scanning out to an area about 12 seconds away shows you trouble early, while there is still time to get ready for it.

guide.label: Searching ahead
guide.text: About 12 seconds. Far enough to plan before a hazard gets close.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Evaluate.

content.question: You just spotted a hazard ahead. What should you do before acting on it?

choices.text: Work out how it could put you at risk, and have a plan
React right away, before spending time thinking it over
Decide who would be at fault if it caused a crash
Wait until it reaches your path before deciding anything

content.explanation: Once you spot a hazard, work out how it could put you at risk and what you will do about it, then act on that plan.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Execute.

content.question: A vehicle ahead seems like it's about to move into your path. Besides changing your speed or position, what else can you do to give yourself room and reduce the danger?

choices.text: Make your presence known with your lights or horn
Hold your line and leave it to the other driver
Wait until the other driver makes eye contact
Stay quiet so you do not startle the other driver

content.explanation: You have three ways to give yourself room and reduce the danger from a hazard: change your speed, change your position or direction, and let others know you are there with your lights or horn.

guide.text: To get room from a hazard, change your speed, change your position or direction, or use your lights or horn to be noticed.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Execute.

content.question: Two hazards are coming up ahead at about the same time. How should you handle them?

choices.text: Adjust your speed to meet them one after the other
Keep a steady speed and pass between them in one move
Watch the larger one and let the smaller one sort itself out
Swerve early so you get around both at once

content.explanation: Slowing down or speeding up lets two hazards spread apart, so you reach them one after the other and can handle each by itself.

guide.text: Two hazards at once: speed up or slow down so you reach them separately.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Intersections.

content.question: A driver ahead is getting ready to cross your path at an intersection. Why cover the clutch and both brakes as you approach?

choices.text: It cuts the time it takes you to react
It makes the motorcycle easier for the driver to see
It steadies your grip over rough pavement in the crossing
It shows the driver that you are about to stop

content.explanation: With the clutch and both brakes covered, less time passes between seeing the driver pull across your path and doing something about it.

guide.text: At an intersection where a vehicle may cross your path, cover the clutch and both brakes. It cuts your reaction time.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Search.

content.question: How far ahead does your immediate path reach, the stretch where a hazard would need a quick swerve or stop?

media.alt: Top-down view of a motorcycle in its lane, with a short shaded band just ahead of it and a second band much farther up the road.

choices.text: About 4 seconds
About 2 seconds
About 8 seconds
About 12 seconds

content.explanation: About 4 seconds is roughly the time and space a swerve or a hard stop needs, so anything inside that range calls for action now.

guide.label: Immediate path
guide.text: About 4 seconds ahead. A hazard inside it needs a quick swerve or stop.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Execute.

content.question: Three or more hazards are ahead of you at once. How should you position yourself among them?

choices.text: Where none of them is closer to you than the rest
Farthest from whichever one is nearest to you
Farthest from moving vehicles, closer to fixed objects
Close behind the vehicle ahead, using it as a shield

content.explanation: Weigh what each hazard could do, then place yourself so that none of them is closer to you than the others.

guide.text: Three or more hazards at once: weigh each one, then keep an equal distance from all of them.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Intersections.

content.question: A car in the oncoming lane signals a left turn into a driveway on a residential street. How should you treat that driveway?

choices.text: With the same care as an intersection
As open road, since it has no sign or signal
As a cue to speed up and get past first
As lower risk, since driveways see little traffic

content.explanation: Any spot where traffic can cut across your path, a driveway included, deserves the care you give an intersection. A car signaling a left turn across you calls for the same approach wherever it happens.

guide.text: Treat any place traffic can cross your path, a driveway included, like an intersection.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Intersections.

content.question: At an intersection, which of these is the biggest danger to a rider?

choices.text: An oncoming car turning left in front of you
A car stopped behind you at a red light
A car beside you going the same way
A pedestrian waiting at the corner to cross

content.explanation: Intersections are where conflict with other traffic is most likely, and an oncoming car turning left in front of you is the biggest danger there. Watch for one as you search the intersection ahead.

guide.label: Biggest danger at an intersection
guide.text: An oncoming car turning left in front of you.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Intersections.

content.question: A driver waiting to pull out at an intersection looks straight at you as you approach. What should you assume?

choices.text: That the driver may still not have seen you
That the driver has seen you and will wait
That you can keep your speed, since you were seen
That the driver has judged your speed correctly

content.explanation: A driver can face your way and still not register a motorcycle. A glance is no promise, so if that car could pull out in front of you, be ready for it to.

guide.text: A driver who seems to look at you may not have seen you. Ride as if they haven't.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Intersections.

content.question: As you approach an intersection, what should decide your lane position?

choices.text: Getting the best view of oncoming traffic
Staying as close to the curb as you can
Tucking in close behind the car ahead
Staying out of sight behind larger vehicles

content.explanation: Choose the part of the lane with the clearest view of oncoming traffic, and ride with your headlight on so drivers can pick you out.

guide.text: Approaching an intersection, keep your headlight on and pick the part of the lane that shows you oncoming traffic best.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Intersections.

content.question: A car coming the other way is waiting to turn left across your lane at the intersection ahead. What should you do as you approach?

choices.text: Slow down and move to where that driver can see you
Speed up to get through before the driver can turn
Keep your speed and line so the driver can judge you
Tuck in behind another vehicle to stay out of the way

content.explanation: Ease off, and choose the part of the lane where that driver is most likely to notice you.

guide.text: When a driver may cross your path, slow down and take a lane position where that driver can see you.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Intersections.

content.question: A car coming the other way is waiting to turn left across your lane at the intersection ahead. As you ride through, which of these should you avoid?

media.alt: Top-down view of a four-way intersection. A motorcycle approaches from the bottom, and a car coming the other way waits in the middle, angled to turn left across the motorcycle's lane.

choices.text: Suddenly changing speed or position
Covering the clutch and both brakes
Easing away from the waiting car
Riding with your headlight on

content.explanation: A sudden change of speed or position can make the waiting driver think you are turning off, and they may start their turn across your lane.

guide.text: Passing a car waiting to turn, avoid sudden changes of speed or position. The driver may think you are turning and pull out.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Intersections.

content.question: As you enter an intersection with traffic close around you, a car coming the other way suddenly turns left across your lane. What is the best response?

choices.text: Brake hard and stop as quickly as you can
Swerve into the next lane to get around it
Speed up to get past before it reaches you
Lay the motorcycle down and slide under it

content.explanation: Hard braking is the move to be ready for when a car coming the other way turns across you, most of all when other traffic is close around you.

guide.text: If a car coming the other way turns left across your lane, be ready to brake hard.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Blind Intersections.

content.question: A parked van on your right hides the cross street at the intersection ahead. Where in your lane should you ride as you approach?

choices.text: The left portion, away from the van
The right portion, tucked in behind the van
The center, since position makes no difference here
Close to the van, so you can see past its front sooner

content.explanation: The side of the lane away from whatever blocks the view is where a driver on the cross street will spot you first. With the van on your right, that is the left portion.

guide.text: At a blind intersection, ride on the side of the lane away from whatever blocks the view, where cross-street drivers see you first.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Blind Intersections.

content.question: You have stopped at the stop line of a blind intersection, and buildings still hide the cross traffic. Where should you stop next to look?

media.alt: Top-down view of a motorcycle stopped at a stop line. Buildings on the near corners hide the street crossing ahead.

choices.text: Just short of the cross lane, with your front wheel out of it
With your front wheel just into the cross lane, for a clearer view
Nowhere; roll out slowly and look as you go
Halfway across the cross lane, where you can see both ways

content.explanation: Creep up and make a second stop right before the cross lane starts, front wheel still clear of it. Then lean forward from the seat to look around whatever is in the way.

guide.text: Blind intersection: stop at the line, then stop again just short of the cross lane, front wheel clear, and lean forward to look.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Passing Parked Cars.

content.question: You are riding past a row of parked cars, and no traffic is coming the other way. Where in your lane should you ride?

choices.text: The left portion, away from the parked cars
The right portion, close to the parked cars
The center, as you would anywhere else
It makes no difference, since the cars are not moving

content.explanation: Keeping to the left portion leaves room for someone stepping out between the cars, a driver getting out, or a door swinging open.

guide.text: Passing parked cars with no oncoming traffic, ride in the left portion, clear of opening doors and people stepping out.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Passing Parked Cars.

content.question: You are passing parked cars while traffic is coming toward you in the other lane. Where in your lane is it usually best to ride?

choices.text: The center, to keep space on both sides
The left portion, as far from the parked cars as you can
The right portion, close to the parked cars
Close behind the car ahead, to stay out of the way

content.explanation: With parked cars on one side and oncoming traffic on the other, the center of the lane keeps a cushion of space on both sides.

guide.text: Passing parked cars with oncoming traffic, the center of the lane usually leaves the most space on both sides.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Passing Parked Cars.

content.question: A car parked at the curb ahead of you starts to pull away. What should you do?

choices.text: Ease off or move over a lane so it has space
Keep your speed, since the driver will check behind first
Speed up to get past before it pulls out
Move closer to the car so its driver can see you

content.explanation: Don't count on the driver having checked behind, or on having noticed you if they did. Give the car space to come out by easing off or moving over.

guide.text: A car pulling away from the curb may not know you're there: ease off or move over.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Passing Parked Cars.

content.question: A car ahead suddenly starts a U-turn that could block the whole road. What should you do?

choices.text: Slow down and sound your horn so the driver knows you're there
Speed up and swerve around the front of the car
Keep your speed and trust the driver to finish the turn
Pull alongside the car so its driver can see you

content.explanation: A car swinging across the road in a U-turn can close off every path past it, and you can't predict how it will move. Bring your speed down, use the horn to make the driver aware of you, and keep your speed low as you go by.

guide.text: A sudden U-turn ahead: slow down and use your horn. The driver's next move is anyone's guess.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Increasing Conspicuity.

content.question: Seen from straight ahead or behind, how does a motorcycle compare with a car?

choices.text: It looks far narrower, so drivers overlook it more easily
It looks about as big, since the rider adds to its size
It stands out more, because drivers rarely see one
It is easier to spot, since its headlight sits up high

content.explanation: Head-on or from behind, a motorcycle presents a thin shape that drivers scanning for cars overlook. It is why so many drivers in these crashes say they never saw the motorcycle.

guide.text: From ahead or behind, a motorcycle is a thin shape drivers easily miss, especially when they're looking for cars.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Increasing Conspicuity.

content.question: A driver sees you coming but pulls out in front of you anyway, sure there is time. What often causes this?

choices.text: Its small size makes it seem farther away than it is
A motorcycle looks closer than it really is
Drivers judge a motorcycle's speed better than a car's
Drivers expect a rider to swerve around them

content.explanation: Size fools the eye: something as small as a motorcycle reads as more distant than it really is. So even a driver who has noticed you can misjudge the gap and pull out.

guide.text: Drivers who do see you can misjudge how close you are, because a small vehicle looks farther off.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Clothing.

content.question: When do most motorcycle crashes happen?

choices.text: In daylight
At night
In rain or fog
On icy winter roads

content.explanation: Most crashes happen in broad daylight, so dress to be seen and keep your headlight on during the day too.

guide.label: When most crashes happen
guide.text: In daylight.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Increasing Conspicuity.

content.question: Which mindset helps a rider stay alert in traffic?

choices.text: Assume other drivers cannot see you
Assume drivers can see you once your headlight is on
Trust a driver who has looked straight at you
Expect drivers to give a motorcycle extra room

content.explanation: Riding as though you are invisible keeps you more alert to what is around you, and quicker to spot trouble coming.

guide.text: Ride as though other drivers cannot see you. It keeps you more alert.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Search.

content.question: What extra risk comes with riding past visually busy surroundings?

choices.text: They make you harder for other drivers to pick out
They make drivers slow down and look out for riders
They block only your own view, not how others see you
They make your headlight stand out more than usual

content.explanation: A busy background of signs and clutter makes a motorcycle harder to pick out. In places like that, assume drivers may miss you.

guide.text: Against a cluttered background, drivers find a motorcycle harder to spot.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Clothing.

content.question: Why does what you wear matter so much for being seen?

choices.text: Your body is about half of the visible rider and motorcycle
Drivers judge a rider's speed by the color of their clothing
A motorcycle cannot be seen at all from straight ahead
Bright clothing does the job of a headlight in daylight

content.explanation: Your body alone accounts for about half of what a driver sees of you and your motorcycle combined, so your clothing does much of the work of getting you noticed.

guide.label: Your share of what drivers see
guide.text: About half of rider and motorcycle together.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Headlight.

content.question: Why keep your headlight on during the day?

choices.text: It makes you about twice as likely to be noticed
It helps you see potholes in bright sunlight
It tells drivers ahead that you are about to turn
It lets drivers judge your speed exactly

content.explanation: Running with the headlight on in the daytime roughly doubles the chance a driver notices you, so leave it on every time you ride.

guide.label: Headlight on by day
guide.text: About twice as likely to be noticed.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Clothing.

content.question: Which jacket gives other drivers the best chance of seeing you?

choices.text: A bright orange one
A black leather one
A light, natural color like tan or khaki
Jacket color has little impact on visibility

content.explanation: Bright orange, red, yellow and green are the easiest colors for drivers to pick out, on a jacket or vest and on your helmet too.

guide.text: Wear a bright orange, red, yellow or green jacket or vest, and a brightly colored helmet.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Clothing.

content.question: A driver is approaching from a side street as you ride through an intersection. What helps that driver spot you?

choices.text: Reflective material on your helmet and vest
The taillight on the back of your motorcycle
A loud exhaust, so the driver hears you coming
A black helmet with a mirrored visor

content.explanation: Reflective strips on the sides of your helmet and on a vest pick up the lights of cross traffic. They help drivers in front of you and behind you see you too.

guide.text: Reflective patches on a vest and on your helmet's sides make you easier to see from every direction, the side most of all.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Headlight.

content.question: Which headlight beam should you use in fog?

choices.text: Low beam
High beam
Parking lights only
No headlight, to cut the glare

content.explanation: In fog, keep your headlight on and switch it to low beam. The light still helps other drivers pick you out, and low beam is the setting for fog.

guide.text: In fog, keep your headlight on, set to low beam.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Signals.

content.question: The road looks empty, and you are about to change lanes. What should you do about signaling?

choices.text: Signal anyway, since it also makes you easier to spot
Skip it, since no one is around to see it
Signal only if you can see a car in your mirror
Signal once you have started moving over

content.explanation: Signals matter even more for a rider, who has less protection than a driver, and a flashing signal also makes you easier to spot. Use one for every lane change and turn.

guide.text: Signal every lane change and turn, even with no one around. Signals also make you easier to spot.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Signals.

content.question: You are merging onto a freeway. How does your turn signal help?

choices.text: Drivers coming from behind are likelier to see you and make room
It lets you skip the mirror and head check before merging
It tells drivers ahead of you to speed up and open a gap
It matters little there, since traffic moves too fast to notice

content.explanation: A blinking signal as you enter a freeway helps drivers approaching from behind notice you in time to make room.

guide.text: Entering a freeway, signal. Drivers coming up from behind are more likely to see you and make room.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Signals.

content.question: You have just finished a turn, and your signal is still blinking. What is the danger?

choices.text: A driver may pull into your path, thinking you will turn again
Drivers behind may tailgate you to get past
It can hide your brake light from drivers behind
None, as long as you keep riding straight

content.explanation: A signal left on after a turn tells drivers you are about to turn again, and one may pull out in front of you on that belief.

guide.text: Switch your signal off after each turn. A driver may pull out, expecting you to turn again.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Brake Light.

content.question: You are about to slow for a turn into an alley in the middle of a block, with traffic behind you. What should you do first?

choices.text: Flash your brake light so drivers behind notice you
Brake suddenly so drivers behind notice the change
Turn on your hazard lights until you are off the road
Skip your turn signal, since a brake light is enough

content.explanation: Drivers following you won't expect a stop partway down a block, and a motorcycle's brake light is small and easy to overlook. A few quick flashes before you start slowing give them warning.

guide.text: Before slowing where drivers behind won't expect it, like partway down a block, flash your brake light. A motorcycle's is easy to miss.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Brake Light.

content.question: A car is following you too closely, and you will need to slow down soon. What should you do before slowing?

choices.text: Flash your brake light
Tap your horn so the driver backs off
Slow down suddenly, so the driver learns to keep back
Watch your mirror closely instead of the road ahead

content.explanation: Flashing the brake light before you slow gives a driver who is too close behind an early warning.

guide.text: When tailgated, flash your brake light before you slow.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Brake Light.

content.question: You are stopped at an intersection, and traffic is coming up behind you. What helps those drivers notice you?

choices.text: Flashing your brake light
Revving your engine so they hear you
Switching on your high beam
Shifting into neutral while you wait

content.explanation: Flashing the brake light while you are stopped helps drivers coming up from behind notice you before they reach you.

guide.text: When stopped at an intersection with traffic coming from behind, flash your brake light.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Using Your Mirrors.

content.question: At which of these moments should you make a special point of checking your mirrors?

choices.text: While stopped at an intersection
In the middle of a sharp curve
While swerving around an obstacle
Just as you cross railroad tracks

content.explanation: Mirror checks are part of your routine search. Three moments call for them most: waiting at an intersection, just before a lane change, and just before you slow.

guide.text: Check mirrors as part of your routine, and above all when waiting at an intersection, before a lane change and before slowing.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Using Your Mirrors.

content.question: Your motorcycle's mirrors are curved outward (convex). How does that change what you see behind you?

choices.text: You see more, but vehicles seem more distant than they are
A wider view, and vehicles look closer than they are
A narrower view, but distances look accurate
The same view as a flat mirror, only brighter

content.explanation: The curve gives you a broader view than flat glass would, but it also makes a car behind you look more distant than it really is.

guide.text: A convex mirror widens your view, and the cars in it are nearer than they look.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Using Your Mirrors.

content.question: You have practiced until you judge distances well in your convex mirrors. What should you still do before changing lanes?

choices.text: Allow extra distance
Trust the mirror, since you have practiced
Skip the head check, since the mirror shows so much
Change lanes quickly, before the gap can close

content.explanation: Practice makes you a better judge of what a convex mirror shows, but leave extra room before a lane change all the same. A good way to practice is to size up a parked car in the mirror while stopped, then turn and look.

guide.text: Even once you judge convex mirrors well, allow extra distance before changing lanes.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Head Checks.

content.question: Why turn your head and look before changing lanes, even after checking your mirrors?

media.alt: Top-down view of a motorcycle in its lane, with an empty lane beside and behind it.

choices.text: Motorcycles have blind spots that mirrors do not show
Turning your head tells drivers you are moving over
Mirrors show only the lane directly behind you
Drivers expect to see a rider look before moving

content.explanation: There are areas beside you that no mirror covers, on a motorcycle just as in a car. A glance over your shoulder at the lane you want is the only way to see them, and doing it often should be routine.

guide.text: A mirror check misses the areas beside you. Look over your shoulder before every lane change.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Head Checks.

content.question: Traffic is moving your way in three or more lanes, and you plan to move one lane to the left. Which lanes should your head check cover?

choices.text: The lane you are moving into and the one beyond it
Only the lane you are moving into
Only the lane behind you, through your mirror
The lane you are moving into and the shoulder on your right

content.explanation: Someone two lanes over may be aiming for the very gap you want. Look across both lanes before you move.

guide.text: On a multi-lane road, check two lanes over before moving: that driver may be headed for your gap.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Horn.

content.question: A car suddenly starts to pull into your path. How should you use your horn?

choices.text: A long, hard blast while you prepare to brake or swerve
One short tap, so you do not startle the driver
Not at all, since braking is all that matters
Sound it, then speed up to get past first

content.explanation: Give one long, strong blast on the horn, and at the same moment get ready to brake hard or steer around the car.

guide.text: Emergency horn use is one long, hard blast while you get ready to brake or swerve.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Horn.

content.question: Why should you never count on your horn alone to keep you safe?

choices.text: It is weaker than a car horn
Drivers tend to ignore a motorcycle's horn
Pressing it means taking a hand off the grip
It is meant only for warning pedestrians

content.explanation: A motorcycle horn is weaker than a car's, so a driver may simply not hear it. Use it when it helps, but never let it be your only plan.

guide.text: Use the horn, but don't make it your only defense: it is weaker than a car's.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Riding at Night.

content.question: You are riding at night on a road you do not know well. How should your speed compare with daytime?

choices.text: Slower than you would ride it by day
The same, as long as your high beam is on
The same, since traffic is usually lighter
A little faster, to spend less time in the dark

content.explanation: Darkness cuts how far you can see and how easily others see you, and a road you don't know holds more surprises. A lower speed buys you time to deal with a hazard.

guide.text: Ride slower at night than by day, especially on roads you don't know.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Riding at Night.

content.question: At night, why should you leave more room when passing or being passed?

choices.text: Distances are harder to judge in the dark
Drivers pass motorcycles more often at night
Traffic usually moves faster after dark
Other drivers cannot see turn signals at night

content.explanation: Judging distance gets harder after dark, so leave a wider margin when you pass someone and when someone passes you.

guide.text: After dark, give passing and being passed extra room, since distances are hard to judge.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Riding at Night.

content.question: Riding at night, you see the taillights of the car ahead bouncing up and down. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The road ahead is bumpy or broken up
The driver is braking hard
The driver is about to turn
The car has a flat tire

content.explanation: The car is riding over an uneven surface you are about to reach. A car ahead helps at night in another way too: its headlights light more of the road than your own high beam does.

guide.text: At night, a car ahead is useful: its lights show you the road, and its taillights bob over rough patches before you reach them.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Riding at Night.

content.question: Riding on a clear night, with no vehicle ahead of you and nothing coming toward you, which beam should you use?

choices.text: High beam
Low beam, so you do not distract anyone
Parking lights only
Low beam, since high beam is for highways only

content.explanation: With no one in front of you and no oncoming traffic, there is nobody to dazzle, so put the high beam on and see as far down the road as you can.

guide.label: High beam at night
guide.text: On until a vehicle is ahead of you or coming toward you.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Riding at Night.

content.question: When is reflective clothing worth wearing?

choices.text: Day and night alike
Only in rain or fog
Only on fast roads like highways
Only on long trips

content.explanation: Reflective material helps drivers pick you out by day as well as after dark, so wear it whenever you ride.

guide.text: Wear reflective material day and night.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Conspicuity, under Riding at Night.

content.question: At night, what should limit your speed?

choices.text: Being able to stop within the distance your headlight lights up
The speed of the traffic around you
The posted speed limit, and nothing else
How far ahead you can see other vehicles' taillights

content.explanation: Your headlight sets the limit. If you need more distance to stop than the beam lights up, you can't stop for something you only just see, so ride slowly enough to pull up inside the lit distance.

guide.text: At night, keep your speed low enough to stop within your headlight's reach.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Crash Avoidance.

content.question: Why does a rider need to be able to swerve, and not only stop quickly?

choices.text: Sometimes there isn't room to stop, or stopping isn't the safest move
A swerve is always safer than a quick stop
Motorcycle brakes tend to fail in an emergency
Swerving is easier to learn than braking hard

content.explanation: Some emergencies leave too little room to stop, or make stopping the riskier choice. Being able to steer around the obstacle gives you a second way out, and knowing which one a moment calls for matters as much as either skill.
