guide.text: Learn to swerve as well as stop: sometimes stopping isn't possible or isn't the safe choice.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Crash Avoidance.

content.question: Studies of riders involved in crashes found a common braking mistake. What was it?

choices.text: Too little front brake and too much rear brake
Too much front brake and too little rear brake
Using both brakes at the same time
Braking too early before a curve

content.explanation: Riders in crashes tend to lean too hard on the rear brake and too little on the front, though the front does most of the stopping. Use the front firmly, with a smooth squeeze rather than a grab.

guide.text: A common crash mistake is too little front brake and too much rear.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Quick Stops.

content.question: During a hard stop, your front wheel locks. What should you do?

choices.text: Release the front brake at once, then reapply it
Keep squeezing the lever until you have stopped
Release both brakes and coast to a stop
Lean back to put more weight on the rear wheel

content.explanation: Let go of the front brake lever right away so the wheel rolls again, then apply the brake again.

guide.text: When the front wheel locks, let go of the front brake at once, then put it back on.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Front-Wheel Skids.

content.question: What does a front-wheel skid cost you the moment it starts?

choices.text: Your steering and your balance
Only some of your braking power
Power from the engine
Nothing, as long as you hold the lever

content.explanation: Once the front wheel locks, you lose steering and balance together. Let go of the lever immediately; holding on means a crash.

guide.text: A locked front wheel takes your steering and balance with it.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Stopping Quickly in a Curve.

content.question: You must stop quickly in a curve, but straightening up first would carry you off the road. How should you brake?

choices.text: Gently at first, then harder as the motorcycle comes upright
As hard as you can, right away, while still leaned over
With the rear brake only, so the front cannot lock
Not at all until you are through the curve

content.explanation: Start with light braking while still leaned, since there is less grip to spare. As speed falls, bring the motorcycle up and squeeze harder as it straightens, reaching full braking once it is upright.

guide.text: Can't straighten before braking in a curve? Brake lightly while leaned, then harder as you come upright.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Stopping Quickly in a Curve.

content.question: You are braking to a stop in a curve. What should you do with the handlebars just before you stop?

choices.text: Straighten them, so you stay balanced and upright
Turn them slightly toward the curb
Keep them turned the way you were leaning
Let them go loose so the front wheel can settle

content.explanation: In the last few feet of the stop, square the handlebars so the motorcycle comes to rest straight up and balanced.

guide.text: Square the handlebars just before you come to a stop in a curve.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Rear-Wheel Skids.

content.question: You press the rear brake so hard that the rear wheel locks. What do you lose right away?

choices.text: The ability to turn or steer away
All of your braking
The use of your front brake
Grip on the front tire

content.explanation: A sliding rear tire won't let the motorcycle change course, and the skid itself can end in a bad crash.

guide.text: Too much rear brake locks the wheel, and while it is locked you can't steer away from trouble.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Swerving or Turning Quickly.

content.question: You need to swerve right around an obstacle, then carry on in your original direction. How do you use the handgrips?

media.alt: Top-down view of a motorcycle approaching an object in its lane, with open space to the right of the object.

choices.text: Press the right grip to swerve, then the left grip once you are clear
Press the left grip to swerve, then the right grip once you are clear
Press the right grip and hold it there until you have stopped
Turn the handlebars right, then let them center on their own

content.explanation: A swerve is two quick presses. Push the right grip and the motorcycle tips right around the obstacle; push the left grip once past it to bring yourself back on course.

guide.text: Swerve with two presses: the grip on the side of your escape, then the other grip to recover.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Swerving or Turning Quickly.

content.question: You are swerving around an obstacle. What should your body do?

choices.text: Stay upright, knees on the tank, as the motorcycle leans under you
Lean with the motorcycle at the same angle, as in a normal turn
Lean the opposite way to keep the motorcycle as upright as possible
Rise off the seat so your knees can absorb the movement

content.explanation: In a swerve, the motorcycle does the leaning, not you. Hold your upper body still and vertical, grip the tank between your knees and keep your feet solid on the footrests while it tips beneath you.

guide.text: In a swerve, your body stays upright while the motorcycle tips beneath you, knees gripping the tank.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Swerving or Turning Quickly.

content.question: As you swerve around an obstacle, where should you look?

choices.text: At your escape path
At the obstacle, so you can judge how far to clear it
Down at the road just ahead of your front tire
In your mirror, to see what is behind you

content.explanation: Your motorcycle goes where your eyes go, so fix your gaze on the gap you're heading for, not on the thing you're avoiding.

guide.text: In a swerve, look at the gap you're aiming for, not at the obstacle.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Swerving or Turning Quickly.

content.question: You have to swerve around an obstacle and slow down as well. When should you brake?

choices.text: Before or after the swerve, never during it
During the swerve, so you slow as you go around
During the swerve, but with the rear brake only
Not at all, since the swerve takes the place of braking

content.explanation: Keep the two apart. Get your braking done before the swerve or save it for after; braking in the middle of a swerve is the thing to avoid.

guide.text: Brake before a swerve or after it, never in the middle of one.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Curves.

content.question: In crashes where a motorcycle is the only vehicle involved, what is one of the leading causes?

choices.text: Failing to hold a curve and running wide
Braking too hard on a straight road
A tire failing at highway speed
Being pushed off line by a crosswind

content.explanation: A rider who can't hold a curve or turn and runs wide, toward the edge or across the line, is behind many of these crashes. Keep your speed within your skill and the posted limit.

guide.text: Many crashes with no other vehicle involved come from a rider failing to hold a curve and running wide.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Curves.

content.question: You are about to ride a curve you have never ridden before. What should you be ready for?

choices.text: It may stay the same, widen, tighten or turn again
It will keep the same sharpness it shows at the entry
It will open up as you go, so you can speed up through it
Its sharpest point will be right at the entry

content.explanation: Curves differ. One holds steady, another opens up, tightens or leads straight into the next bend, so watch how it develops and keep your speed within your skill and the posted limit.

guide.text: No two curves are alike: a curve may hold steady, open up, tighten or turn again.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Curves.

content.question: How should you choose your path through a curve?

choices.text: Pick your position to suit traffic, the surface and the curve's shape
Follow the curve of the road, since it is built as the safest line
Take whichever line lets you keep your speed up
Follow the line of the vehicle ahead of you

content.explanation: There is no single correct line. Where you ride in the lane through a curve depends on what traffic is doing, what is on the road surface and how the curve bends.

guide.text: Your line through a curve needn't follow the road's own curve; set it for traffic and conditions.

meta.sourceSection: The Rider and the Motorcycle.

content.question: How does a motorcycle compare with a car in the way it handles?

choices.text: It responds faster, but rough roads and crosswinds affect it more
It responds faster, and its small size lets it shrug off crosswinds
It responds more slowly, so it needs more room to change direction
It handles much like a car once it is moving

content.explanation: A motorcycle reacts to your inputs more quickly than a car does. It is also pushed around more by things outside your control, such as bumpy pavement and gusts from the side.

guide.text: Quicker to respond than a car, a motorcycle is also more easily upset by rough pavement and side winds.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles.

content.question: You can't avoid riding over a small obstacle in the road. What should you do as you reach it?

choices.text: Stand up a little and add a touch of throttle just before you hit it
Stay firmly in the seat and brake hard just as your front tire reaches it
Stand up a little and brake hard as the front tire meets it
Stay seated and pull in the clutch so the motorcycle coasts across it

content.explanation: Get your speed as low as you can and the motorcycle straight before you reach it. Lift your weight onto the footrests so your legs and arms soak up the bump, and give a quick blip of throttle just before the front tire hits to lighten it.

guide.text: Over an obstacle: slow down, straighten up, stand slightly on the footrests and add a little throttle just before contact.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles.

content.question: You have just ridden over an object in the road, and the motorcycle still feels normal. What should you do?

choices.text: Get off the road and look over the tires and wheels
Keep riding, since any damage would already show in the handling
Check the tires at your next fuel stop
Ride a short way faster to test the steering

content.explanation: Pull off and look over both tires and wheels before you ride any more, whatever the handling feels like.

guide.text: Hit something in the road? Stop somewhere safe and look over the tires and wheels before riding on.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: When is wet pavement especially slippery?

choices.text: When rain first starts, before the surface oil has washed away
After hours of steady rain have soaked the road surface
Once the rain has stopped and the road begins to dry out
Only where water has pooled deep enough to form puddles

content.explanation: The first rain is the worst, because the oil on the road hasn't yet been rinsed toward the edges. Painted lines, steel plates and metal covers also turn slick when wet.

guide.label: Wet pavement at its slickest
guide.text: Just after rain starts, while oil is still on the surface.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: There is a wet curve ahead. When should you slow down?

choices.text: Before you reach the curve
Once you are leaned into it, with gentle braking
Only if the tires start to slide
As you exit, once the motorcycle is upright

content.explanation: Shed your speed before a slippery stretch, not on it, since stopping takes longer there and a skid is more likely. A wet curve is where this matters most.

guide.text: Get your speed down before you reach a slick surface, above all a wet curve.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: On a slippery surface, what can cause a skid?

choices.text: Any abrupt input, whether braking, steering, throttle or shifting
Hard braking, but not a sudden turn
A sudden turn, but not hard braking
Only shifting gears too quickly

content.explanation: There is little grip to spare on a slick road, and a jerk on any control can use it up. Brake, steer, shift and roll the throttle as gently as you can.

guide.text: On slick roads, be gentle with every control. Anything abrupt can start a skid.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: You need to slow down on a wet, slippery road. How should you use the front brake?

choices.text: Use it, squeezing gradually so the wheel does not lock
Leave it alone and slow with the rear brake only
Squeeze it hard so the tire bites through the water
Pump it quickly on and off to keep the wheel turning

content.explanation: Don't give up on the front brake on a wet road; it still does real work. Use both brakes, with a slow, gentle squeeze on the front lever so its wheel doesn't lock.

guide.text: On a wet road, keep using the front brake, squeezing it gently.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles.

content.question: You must ride over a small obstacle you could not avoid. At what angle should you approach it?

choices.text: Square to it, or as near square as you can get
At a shallow angle, so the tire rolls onto it gradually
At a slant, so the front tire glances off it
Angle does not matter if you slow down first

content.explanation: Hit it head-on, at or close to 90 degrees, rather than glancing across it, and keep your eyes up on the path beyond it.

guide.text: Meet an unavoidable obstacle square on, as close to 90 degrees as you can.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: Rain has just begun. Which part of your lane gives the best footing?

choices.text: A tire track, often the left one
The middle, away from the tire tracks
Near the edge, close to the shoulder
Always in the right tire track, nearest the curb

content.explanation: Once rain starts, the oily strip down the center of the lane turns slick, so ride where car tires run instead. Of those two tracks, the left is often better, depending on traffic and the road.

guide.text: In early rain, stay off the slick center strip and ride a tire track, often the left.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: You are coming to a stop at a busy intersection. What should you check before putting your foot down?

choices.text: That there is no oil spot where it will land
That it lands on the painted stop line, which gives the best grip
That it lands on loose grit, which keeps your boot from sliding
Nothing, as long as the motorcycle has fully stopped

content.explanation: Look at where your boot will land before you put it down at a stop or when parking. An oil spot can make it slide out from under you, and you can fall.

guide.text: Check for oil wherever your foot will land when you stop or park.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: Where do dirt and gravel tend to collect on a paved road?

choices.text: Near the edges, and worst on curves and ramps
In the center of the lane, between the tire tracks
On bridges and overpasses
Evenly across the lane, wherever traffic is light

content.explanation: Debris settles at the edges of the road, and curves and freeway ramps gather the most. Keep an eye on the road's edge in those places.

guide.text: Loose gravel gathers at the edges of the road, worst on curves and ramps.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: On a cold day, where are patches of ice most likely to form?

choices.text: Low or shaded spots, and bridges and overpasses
On sunny stretches, where snow has melted first
Evenly across the road, wherever it is wet
Mostly on gravel roads rather than paved ones

content.explanation: Watch for ice in dips, in shade, and on bridges and overpasses. A road doesn't thaw evenly, so a clear stretch doesn't mean the next one is clear.

guide.label: Where to expect ice
guide.text: Shady spots and dips, and bridges and overpasses.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: You cannot avoid a stretch of ice or snow. How should you ride across it?

choices.text: Straight up, very slowly and without braking
Leaned slightly, with steady pressure on the rear brake
Briskly, so you spend as little time on it as possible
In a low gear, with bursts of throttle for grip

content.explanation: Keep the motorcycle vertical, crawl across and leave the brakes alone. At walking pace you can let your feet brush the surface to steady yourself, and pull the clutch in to roll if you can. Better still, keep off icy or snowy roads.

guide.text: If you must cross ice or snow, stay upright, go as slowly as you can and don't brake.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams.

content.question: Railroad tracks cross your road at an angle. How should you usually cross them?

media.alt: Top-down view of a motorcycle approaching railroad tracks that cross its lane at a slant, with a second lane beside it.

choices.text: Straight across, staying in your lane
Turn so you cross them at a right angle
Swerve across them at the last moment
Edge across slowly, one tire at a time

content.explanation: Stay in your own lane and ride over the railroad tracks on your normal line. Turning to hit them square on sounds safer but can steer you into another lane.

guide.text: Ride straight over angled railroad tracks without leaving your lane; turning to square up can take you into another lane.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams.

content.question: A railroad or trolley track, or a pavement seam, runs alongside your path, and you need to cross it. What should you do?

media.alt: Top-down view of a motorcycle riding just beside a pavement seam that runs along its lane.

choices.text: Move away, then cross at 45 degrees or more with a decisive turn
Edge across it gradually, keeping the angle as shallow as possible
Brake firmly just as your front tire meets the seam
Steer onto it and ride along it until it fades out

content.explanation: A rail or seam running the same way you are can trap a tire that creeps over it at a shallow angle. Give yourself room first, then turn across it firmly at 45 degrees or steeper.

guide.text: To cross a rail or seam running alongside you, open some distance, then turn across it firmly at 45 degrees or more.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Grooves and Gratings.

content.question: Riding over a bridge grating, you feel the motorcycle start to weave. What should you do?

choices.text: Hold your speed and go straight across
Slow down sharply until the weaving stops
Turn to cross at an angle and get off it sooner
Grip the bars tightly and steer against the weave

content.explanation: That wandering feel over a grating or grooved pavement is normal and not dangerous in itself. Keep a steady throttle and a straight line. Crossing at an angle is what gets riskier, because you have to keep correcting back into your lane.

guide.text: Over grates or grooves, a little weaving is normal: keep your speed and ride straight across.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tire Failure.

content.question: How can you usually tell that a tire has gone flat, and which one?

choices.text: By the handling: heavy steering means the front, jerking or swaying means the rear
By the handling: heavy steering means the rear, jerking or swaying means the front
By the bang or hiss, which you will hear from the side that failed
You can't tell until you stop and look at the tires

content.explanation: Tire failures are usually silent, so a sudden change in how the motorcycle handles is the clue. Steering that feels heavy points to the front, and that one is the more dangerous, because steering is how you stay balanced. A rear that wags or slides about points to the back.

guide.text: A flat is usually silent: heavy steering means the front tire, a wagging tail means the rear.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tire Failure.

content.question: A tire goes flat while you are riding. What should you do first?

choices.text: Hold the grips firmly, roll off gently and steer straight
Brake hard with both brakes to stop as quickly as you can
Pull in the clutch at once and steer for the shoulder
Speed up slightly to keep the motorcycle stable

content.explanation: With a flat, control comes first: hold the grips firmly, roll off the throttle gently and keep the motorcycle running straight. Once it has slowed, ease over to the roadside, pull in the clutch and stop.

guide.text: With a flat: grip firmly, roll off gently and steer straight, then once slowed, move to the roadside, pull in the clutch and stop.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tire Failure.

content.question: Your rear tire has gone flat and you need to slow down. How should you brake?

choices.text: Gradually, with the front brake only
Firmly with both brakes, as in any quick stop
With the rear brake only, to spare the good tire
Hard with the front brake, since it does most of the stopping

content.explanation: Brake only with the wheel whose tire still holds air, building the pressure gradually, and only if you are certain which tire is flat. With the rear flat, that means the front brake.

guide.text: With a flat, brake gently using only the wheel whose tire is still good, and only if you know which tire has gone.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Stuck Throttle.

content.question: Your throttle sticks open, and twisting it back and forth does not free it. What should you do?

choices.text: Hit the engine cut-off switch while pulling in the clutch
Pull in the clutch and let the engine rev until the cable frees
Brake hard and keep the engine running so you still have power
Keep twisting the throttle until the cable frees itself

content.explanation: Kill the engine with its cut-off switch while pulling the clutch in, which takes drive away from the rear wheel at once. The engine may keep sounding busy for a moment; that's normal. Then pull over somewhere safe, and inspect the throttle cable before riding again.

guide.text: If twisting won't free a stuck throttle, kill the engine with its cut-off switch, pull in the clutch and stop.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Wobble.

content.question: Without warning, your handlebars and front wheel begin shaking side to side. What is the usual cause?

choices.text: Wrong tire pressure, the load, or unsuitable accessories
A rear tire that is slowly losing its air pressure
Using the front brake on its own at low speed
Riding in too high a gear for the speed you are going

content.explanation: That shake is called a wobble, and most come from how the motorcycle is set up: tire pressure that is off, a load carried badly, or an accessory that doesn't suit it. If correcting those doesn't stop it, have the steering and front wheel looked at.

guide.text: A wobble, the bars shaking side to side, usually starts with tire pressure, the load or a poorly suited accessory.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Wobble.

content.question: Your front wheel and handlebars start shaking from side to side. How should you respond?

choices.text: Hold the bars firmly without fighting the shake, and ease off the throttle
Speed up, since more speed steadies the front end
Steer firmly against each shake to cancel it out
Loosen your grip and let the front wheel settle itself

content.explanation: Keep a firm hold but let the bars move rather than wrestling them, and roll off the throttle slowly. Don't brake, which can make the shaking worse, and don't try to power out of it. Shift your weight forward and down, then leave the road at the first chance and find the cause.

guide.text: In a wobble: a firm grip, no fighting the bars, a slow roll off the throttle and no brakes, then pull over.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Drive Train Problems.

content.question: Your drive chain breaks while you are riding. What will you notice, and what should you do?

choices.text: The rear wheel loses all drive; roll off and brake to a stop
Heavy steering at the front; hold a straight line and ease off
The engine stalls at once; restart it and ride on carefully
Nothing at first; keep riding and check the chain at your next stop

content.explanation: You'll feel the power vanish from the rear wheel all at once. Roll off, brake and stop in a safe spot. A slipping or broken chain or belt can also jam the rear wheel and skid it, which is why it pays to keep the drive adjusted.

guide.text: A snapped chain or belt kills drive instantly. Roll off, brake and pull over somewhere safe.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Engine Seizure.

content.question: Your engine suddenly loses power and starts to sound different, a sign it may be seizing. What should you do?

choices.text: Squeeze the clutch, pull off the road and check the oil
Open the throttle to keep the engine turning over
Shift down a gear to bring the engine speed up
Keep riding gently until you reach a service station

content.explanation: An engine that seizes is usually short of oil, and its parts start to bind. Disconnect it from the rear wheel with the clutch, get off the road and check the oil level, and let it cool before trying to restart.

guide.text: If the engine starts to seize, squeeze the clutch, pull off and check the oil.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Animals.

content.question: You are riding in traffic when a small animal darts into your lane. What should you do?

choices.text: Stay in your lane, avoiding it only if you safely can
Swerve into the next lane to miss it
Swerve onto the shoulder to miss it
Brake as hard as you can, even with cars close behind you

content.explanation: Swerving out of your lane to miss the animal can put you into a car, which is far more dangerous to you than the animal is. Avoid it within your lane if you safely can; if you can't, hitting it is the lesser risk.

guide.text: In traffic, stay in your lane for an animal: hitting it is safer for you than hitting a car.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Animals.

content.question: A dog starts chasing your motorcycle. What should you do?

choices.text: Slow down and downshift, then accelerate away as you reach it
Sound the horn and hold your speed until it gives up
Brake hard so it runs on past you
Speed up at once to outrun it before it gets close

content.explanation: Ease off and drop a gear as the dog comes at you, then open the throttle as you draw level and leave it behind. Keep both feet up and your eyes on where you're going, not on the dog.

guide.text: Chased by a dog: slow and downshift, then accelerate away as you reach it. Never kick at it.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Animals.

content.question: A deer is standing beside the road ahead. What should you do?

choices.text: Slow down and be ready to stop, since it could move any way
Downshift, approach slowly, then speed up past it
Sound your horn and hold your speed
Swerve wide around it without slowing

content.explanation: There's no telling which way a deer, elk or cow will go, so slow down and be ready to stop.

guide.text: Deer, elk and cattle can move any way at any time: slow down and be ready to stop.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Flying Objects.

content.question: A pebble kicked up by the vehicle ahead hits your face shield hard. What should you do?

choices.text: Keep looking ahead and keep both hands on the grips
Lift the shield right away to check it for damage
Brake hard and stop right where you are
Turn your head away in case more stones follow

content.explanation: A hit from a stone or a bug is startling, but steady control matters more than the shield. Stay focused on the road and keep both hands on the bars, then deal with any damage once you can pull off safely.

guide.text: Hit by a stone or insect? Keep your eyes forward and both hands on the bars, and stop later to check for damage.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Getting Off the Road.

content.question: You need to pull off the road to check your motorcycle. What should you do before you turn off?

choices.text: Check the ground is firm, then signal and check mirror and blind spot
Brake firmly and early so the driver behind sees your brake light
Turn off quickly so you spend less time slowing down in traffic
Wait until you are safely on the shoulder before you signal

content.explanation: Look at the shoulder first: if it is grass, sand or anything you're unsure of, slow right down before you leave the pavement. Signal early so traffic behind knows you're slowing and turning, and do a mirror and shoulder check before you move.

guide.text: Leaving the road: judge the shoulder first, then signal and check behind you before turning off.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Getting Off the Road.

content.question: You have pulled off the road to rest. Where should you stop the motorcycle?

choices.text: Well clear of the road, on firm, level ground
Right at the edge of the pavement, where drivers can see you
Close to the pavement, so you can pull back out easily
On the sloped part of the shoulder, so rain drains away

content.explanation: A motorcycle parked at the edge of the road is hard for passing drivers to see, and someone else may pull off right where you are. Get as far from traffic as you can, onto ground firm and flat enough to hold the stand.

guide.text: Pull far off the road onto firm, flat ground: a roadside motorcycle is hard to see, and soft or sloped shoulders won't hold a stand.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Carrying Passengers and Cargo.

content.question: Who should carry a passenger or a large load?

choices.text: Only experienced riders, since the weight changes the handling
Any licensed rider, since a passenger barely changes the handling
New riders, so they can get used to the extra weight early
Only riders whose motorcycle has a larger engine

content.explanation: A passenger or a heavy load alters how the motorcycle handles, so carrying either is for experienced riders, and even they should practice with the added weight first.

guide.text: Carrying a passenger or heavy load is for experienced riders; the added weight alters the handling.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Equipment for Carrying a Passenger.

content.question: What protective gear should your passenger wear?

choices.text: Gear as protective as your own
A helmet, with lighter gear than yours elsewhere
Whatever they find comfortable for a short ride
Less than you, since you shield them from the wind

content.explanation: A passenger is just as exposed as you are, so their protective gear should match yours.

guide.text: Your passenger's protective gear should match yours.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: Where should a child passenger sit?

choices.text: Directly behind the rider
In front of the rider, where you can keep hold of them
In front of the rider, so you can see them at all times
Either place, as long as they can reach a footrest

content.explanation: Behind you is the only safe place for a child. In front, a child can't keep their balance well and may get in the way of your steering and controls.

guide.text: A child passenger sits directly behind the rider, never in front.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: Your passenger rides a motorcycle of their own. Should you still give them instructions before you set off?

choices.text: Yes, always give complete instructions before you start
No, a rider already knows what a passenger should do
Only if they have never been a passenger before
Only if the trip will include highway riding

content.explanation: Brief every passenger before you set off, riders included. Knowing how to ride a motorcycle isn't the same as knowing how to be a passenger on one.

guide.text: Always instruct your passenger before setting off, even one who rides.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: Your passenger is about to climb on. How should you have the motorcycle ready?

choices.text: Engine running in neutral, both your feet down, brake on
Engine off, with the side stand down to hold it steady
Engine running in first gear, ready to pull away
Engine running, with you still standing beside it

content.explanation: Start the engine and select neutral before your passenger gets on, then brace the motorcycle with both feet planted and the brake on while they climb aboard.

guide.text: Start the engine and find neutral before a passenger mounts, and hold the motorcycle steady with both feet down and the brake on.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: Where should your passenger sit, and what should they hold on to?

choices.text: Well forward, without crowding you, holding your waist, hips or belt
Upright and apart from you, hands resting on their knees
Wherever is comfortable, holding on to your shoulders
Pressed against you, gripping your arms for balance

content.explanation: Your passenger should sit well forward, but not so close that they cramp your control, and hold on at your waist, hips or belt.

guide.text: Passengers sit well forward without crowding you and hold your waist, hips or belt.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: What should your passenger do with their feet and legs?

choices.text: Keep their feet on the footrests at all times and their legs away from the exhaust
Put their feet down at stops to help you hold the motorcycle up
Let their legs hang loose so they can help balance the motorcycle
Lift their feet off the footrests whenever you turn

content.explanation: A passenger who puts a foot down at a stop can lose their footing and pull you over with them, so their feet stay on the footrests the whole time. Their legs need to stay away from the hot exhaust and from moving parts like the chain.

guide.text: Passengers keep their feet on the footrests the whole ride and their legs away from the exhaust and chain.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: How should your passenger ride through a turn?

choices.text: Lined up behind you, looking past your shoulder toward the turn
Leaning the opposite way to help balance the motorcycle
Turned partway around, watching traffic behind you
Looking straight ahead at the middle of your back

content.explanation: Turning together works best when the passenger stays lined up behind you and watches the turn over your shoulder. That keeps their lean matched to yours.

guide.text: In turns, a passenger stays lined up behind you and looks past your shoulder toward the turn.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: When should your passenger tighten their hold on you?

choices.text: Before bumps, when pulling away, and before any sharp or sudden move
Only when you are braking hard for a stop
Only once you are up to highway speed
Never, since a tight hold makes it hard for you to steer

content.explanation: Warn your passenger to grip harder at the moments the motorcycle jolts or shifts: rough patches in the road, pulling away from a stop, and sharp turns or sudden moves. The rest of the time they should sit still and keep talk to a minimum.

guide.text: Tell your passenger to hold on tighter for bumps, pull-aways and sharp moves.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Riding With Passengers.

content.question: How does a heavier passenger change the way your motorcycle responds?

choices.text: Everything takes longer: accelerating, stopping and turning
It stops sooner, since the weight presses the tires down
It turns more quickly, since the weight helps it lean
It makes little difference once you are moving

content.explanation: Extra weight makes the motorcycle slower to respond to everything you ask of it, and the heavier the passenger, the more you'll notice it.

guide.text: With a heavy passenger, expect the motorcycle to take longer to accelerate, stop and turn.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Riding With Passengers.

content.question: You are carrying a passenger. How should you change the way you ride?

choices.text: Ease your pace, brake sooner and take only bigger gaps in traffic
Ride a little faster, so the extra weight keeps you stable
Brake later and harder, since the weight helps you stop
Ride just as you would alone

content.explanation: Two-up, give everything more margin. Take curves, corners and bumps a bit slower, begin braking sooner and keep more space when you slow, and wait for a bigger gap before crossing, joining or merging with traffic.

guide.text: With a passenger, slow down a little, brake sooner, keep more space and wait for bigger gaps.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Motorcycle.

content.question: You are about to carry a passenger for the first time. What should you adjust on the motorcycle?

choices.text: Both tire pressures and the suspension, for the extra weight
Only the rear tire, since that is where the weight goes
Nothing, as long as you stay within the weight limit
The handlebars, raised to give the passenger room

content.explanation: Extra weight calls for setup changes: set both tires, front as well as rear, to the pressures your owner's manual gives, and adjust the suspension for the load.

guide.text: Before carrying a passenger or heavy load, check both tire pressures and adjust the suspension for the weight.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo.

content.question: Where should you carry a heavy load on your motorcycle?

media.alt: Side view of a motorcycle and rider, with the area over and behind the rear axle empty.

choices.text: Low down, and no farther back than the rear axle
High on a rack behind the seat, out of the way
Behind the rear axle, to balance a passenger's weight
All in one saddlebag, so it is easy to reach

content.explanation: Weight carried high makes the motorcycle top-heavy and less stable, and weight hung behind the rear axle changes how it turns and brakes and can start a wobble. Keep the load low and toward the middle, and split it evenly between saddlebags so the motorcycle doesn't pull to one side.

guide.text: Load low, no farther back than the rear axle, with saddlebags evenly weighted.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo.

content.question: What is the best way to fasten a load to your motorcycle?

choices.text: Bungee cords or nets, hooked at two or more points on each side
Rope, pulled tight and tied off with strong knots
A single strap run across the top of the load
Loosely, so the load can shift with the motorcycle

content.explanation: Stretchy bungee cords or a cargo net, hooked at several points on each side, keep a load from shifting. Rope stretches and knots work loose, and a load that slips can jam in the wheel or chain and lock it. Stop now and then to check it's still tight.

guide.text: Secure loads with bungee cords or nets at several points per side, and recheck them on the way.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo.

content.question: You are mounting a tank bag. What should you make sure of?

choices.text: It is secure and clear of the controls and brake lines
It sits high enough on the tank to be easy to reach
It is packed completely full so nothing shifts inside
It is strapped loosely so it can move with the steering

content.explanation: Strap the bag on firmly where it won't hide the instruments or get in the way of the controls, and pack it lightly if that's what it takes. Check the straps don't snag a brake line or cable around the steering head.

guide.text: Strap a tank bag down tight, clear of the controls, gauges and brake lines.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Pre-Ride Test.

content.question: Your motorcycle is fully loaded for a trip. What should you do before setting out?

choices.text: Ride it somewhere quiet first to get a feel for the load
Head straight for the highway so the load can settle
Nothing more, once the load is strapped down
Test the brakes with a hard stop in traffic

content.explanation: A full load changes how the motorcycle feels, so try it out somewhere quiet before the real trip. Make sure nothing drags in turns or over bumps and the steering moves freely, and expect it to accelerate more slowly and need more room to stop.

guide.text: Before a trip, try out the loaded motorcycle on quiet roads; it will be slower to speed up and to stop.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Before a group ride, why should every rider know the route?

choices.text: So a separated rider never has to hurry
So the group can do without a lead rider
So the riders can take turns in the lead
So the group can skip the planned rest stops

content.explanation: Talk the ride through before you leave: the route, how long each leg is, the rest stops, and where to stop for fuel, food and the night. A rider who loses the group but knows where it is going can take their time instead of rushing to catch up.

guide.text: Go over the route and stops before a group ride, so anyone who gets separated can rejoin without rushing.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: On a group ride, which rider sets the pace for the group?

choices.text: The last rider in the group
The lead rider, riding up front
Each rider, at their own safe speed
Whichever rider planned the route

content.explanation: Pace is set from the back, by the last rider. The front and back positions both go to the group's most experienced riders, and the leader's job is watching ahead and signaling early enough that the whole line hears about changes in good time.

guide.text: In a group, the rider at the back sets the pace, and the most experienced riders take the front and the back.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: On a group ride, where should the least experienced riders ride?

choices.text: Near the front, right behind the leader
At the back, where they set no pace for others
In the middle, with experienced riders on every side
Wherever they feel comfortable, so long as they keep up

content.explanation: New riders go second, right behind the leader. From there they never have to race to keep up, and the riders behind them can keep an eye on how they're doing.

guide.text: Put the least experienced riders directly behind the leader, where they won't need to chase the group.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: A rider in your group wants to go faster than the others. What should they do?

choices.text: Head off on their own and meet the group at an agreed stop
Pass the other riders whenever it is safe
Ride close behind the leader to pick up the pace
Ask the whole group to speed up to match

content.explanation: A group ride is not a race. Riders don't pass one another inside the group except in an emergency, and nobody crowds or hurries the rider in front. Anyone who wants a faster pace rides on ahead and waits at a meeting point agreed beforehand.

guide.text: In a group, nobody races, passes inside the group or crowds the rider ahead. A faster rider goes on to an agreed meeting point.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: On a group ride, you see in your mirror that the rider behind you has fallen well back. What should the group do?

choices.text: The whole group eases off until it is back together
Keep the pace, since every rider knows the route
Only the last rider drops back to stay with them
Pull over right away and wait on the shoulder

content.explanation: Each rider keeps an eye in the mirror on the person behind, and when someone drops back, the group slows as one so nobody is left behind. If some riders struggle with the pace in curves, set it by the least experienced rider, or split into two groups.

guide.text: Keep the rider behind you in your mirror, and if someone falls back, the whole group eases off.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: What is one advantage of a group riding in close ranks?

choices.text: Other drivers can see the group more easily
Riders can talk to one another as they ride
Each rider can do without a space cushion
The leader can hold a faster pace for everyone

content.explanation: A tight group is easier for drivers to see, uses less of the road and is harder for traffic to break up. Tight doesn't mean crowded, though: every rider still needs space and time to react.

guide.text: Riding close together makes a group easier to see and harder to split, but each rider still needs a space cushion.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Is it safe for two riders in a group to ride side by side in the same lane?

choices.text: No, it leaves neither rider an escape route
Yes, if both riders hold exactly the same speed
Yes, on a multi-lane highway in light traffic
Only when the riders need to talk to each other

content.explanation: Two motorcycles abreast in one lane box each other in: if a car or debris appears, neither has anywhere to go. Save conversations for when you've both stopped.

guide.text: Never ride two abreast in one lane; neither rider would have room to dodge a hazard.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: In a staggered group formation, where in the lane does the leader ride?

choices.text: The left side, with the second rider on the right
The right side, with the second rider on the left
The center, with the others in single file behind
Beside the second rider, so both can be seen

content.explanation: Staggering puts the leader toward the left of the lane and the next rider toward the right, behind them, and the pattern repeats down the group. No two riders are ever side by side.

guide.label: Staggered formation
guide.text: The leader rides the left of the lane, the second rider the right, and so on, alternating.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Your group is riding in a staggered formation. When should it move into single file?

choices.text: In curves, turns, and entering or leaving a highway
Whenever the traffic around the group gets heavy
When cruising on a long, straight stretch of highway
Whenever one of the riders falls behind the group

content.explanation: Go to single file for curves and turns and at highway entrances and exits, then stagger again once you're through.

guide.text: A staggered group goes single file for curves, turns and highway entrances and exits.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Your group is riding in a staggered formation and needs to pass a slower car, using the oncoming lane. How should it pass?

choices.text: One rider at a time, each when it is safe
All together, close behind the leader
Two at a time, to cut time in the oncoming lane
The leader first, then everyone else at once

content.explanation: Through the oncoming lane, pass singly. The leader goes when it's clear, then the next rider moves to the left of the lane and waits for their own safe chance, and so on down the group. Each rider judges the oncoming traffic for themselves.

guide.text: A staggered group passes through the oncoming lane one rider at a time, each from the left of the lane when it's clear.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Your group is passing a slower car one rider at a time. After the leader passes, where in the lane should the leader ride?

media.alt: Top-down view of a group of motorcycles in staggered formation behind a car, with the leader pulling out to pass.

choices.text: The left side, holding passing speed
The right side, to make room for the next rider
The center, slowing so the others catch up
Whichever side has the better view ahead

content.explanation: The leader settles back into the left of the lane, the usual lead spot, and keeps up passing speed so there is room for the next rider to come in behind. Each rider then returns to their own place in the formation.

guide.text: Once past, the leader takes the left of the lane again and keeps the speed up to make room behind.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Alcohol and Drugs in Motorcycle Operation.

content.question: You have had one drink and are well under the legal limit. Can it affect your riding?

choices.text: Yes, even one drink can affect it
No, not until you reach the legal limit
Not if you are used to drinking
Only if you start to feel its effects

content.explanation: A single drink is enough to change how you ride. Judgment and skill start to slip long before you reach the legal limit, and alcohol dulls your thinking along with your physical control.

guide.text: Even one drink can affect your riding. Impairment begins well below the legal limit.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Alcohol and Drugs in Motorcycle Operation.

content.question: You took an over-the-counter cold medicine this morning. What should you know before riding?

choices.text: Its side effects could make riding riskier
Over-the-counter drugs don't affect riding
It is safe as long as you haven't been drinking
It is fine if you ride slowly and carefully

content.explanation: Plenty of medicines, bought over the counter or prescribed, can affect how well you ride, as can illegal drugs. Mixing any of them with alcohol is worse than either on its own.

guide.text: Medicines from the shelf or the pharmacy can make riding riskier, and alcohol on top makes it worse.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Blood Alcohol Concentration.

content.question: Which three things do the most to decide your blood alcohol concentration?

choices.text: How much you drink, how fast, and your body weight
The time of day, the weather, and your mood
Your age, your height, and how long you have ridden
The brand, the price, and how cold it is

content.explanation: BAC measures how much alcohol is in your blood. The biggest influences are the number of drinks, how quickly you have them and how much you weigh, and drinking faster leaves more of it in your system.

guide.text: BAC, the alcohol in your blood, depends mainly on how much you drink, how fast, and your weight.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Blood Alcohol Concentration.

content.question: Which holds the most alcohol: a 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine or a shot of liquor?

choices.text: None; they hold about the same
The shot, since liquor is the strongest
The beer, since it is the largest
The wine, since it is stronger than beer

content.explanation: Each counts as one drink: a standard beer (12 ounces), a glass of wine (5 ounces) and a single shot of liquor all carry roughly the same alcohol.

guide.label: One drink
guide.text: A 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine or one shot of liquor, each about the same alcohol.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Blood Alcohol Concentration.

content.question: About how quickly does your body process alcohol?

choices.text: About one drink an hour
About two drinks an hour
About three drinks an hour
Faster with coffee or a cold shower

content.explanation: Your body processes alcohol at about one drink an hour. Drink faster than that and the alcohol builds up, raising your BAC.

guide.label: How fast your body clears alcohol
guide.text: About one drink an hour. Drink faster and it builds up.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Minimize the Risks.

content.question: Which ability does alcohol affect first?

choices.text: Your sense of how well you're riding
Seeing clearly, as your vision blurs
Keeping your balance at low speeds
Hearing horns and sirens around you

content.explanation: The first thing to go is your ability to rate yourself. You feel sharper while actually riding worse, and the false confidence leads you to take bigger chances.

guide.text: Drinking first spoils your sense of how well you're riding: you feel better as you ride worse.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Make an Intelligent Choice.

content.question: You'll be riding home later. Why is setting yourself a drink limit a poor plan?

choices.text: Drinking makes it harder to stick to the limit
A limit is only a problem for new riders
It isn't; a limit keeps you under the legal BAC
It isn't, as long as you pace your drinks

content.explanation: Alcohol works on the very judgment you'd need to stop at your limit. If you are riding, skip the drinks; if you have been drinking, find another way home.

guide.text: Planning to ride? Don't drink, because limits are hard to keep once you start. Been drinking? Don't ride.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Make an Intelligent Choice.

content.question: Before riding, you waited an hour for each drink you had. Which is true?

choices.text: You may still feel the effects
A cup of coffee will clear anything left over
You are certain to be back under the legal limit
Whatever remains is too little to matter

content.explanation: An hour a drink is a rough rule, not a guarantee. Bodies clear alcohol at different rates, and the tiredness that follows drinking can outlast the alcohol itself, so give it longer.

guide.text: An hour per drink is no guarantee you're fit to ride; the effects can linger.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Step In to Protect a Friend.

content.question: A friend has had too much to drink and is about to ride home. What should you do?

choices.text: Intervene and stop them riding
Let them decide, since it is their choice
Follow them home to make sure they are safe
Tell them to ride slowly and carefully

content.explanation: Someone who is drunk is in no state to decide for themselves, which leaves it to the people around them. Get them a ride, slow down the drinking, find reasons to keep them there, take the keys if you can and bring other friends in to help.

guide.text: A drunk friend can't make the call to ride, so make it for them: arrange a ride, keep them there, take the key.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Cannabis & Motorcycle Operation.

content.question: Even where cannabis is legal, why is it unsafe to ride after using it?

choices.text: It warps your judgment of time, distance and speed
It is only unsafe when combined with alcohol
It is only unsafe if it was eaten, not smoked
Its effects wear off within a few minutes

content.explanation: Legal or not, riding while impaired by cannabis is against the law and unsafe, because it throws off how you judge time, distance and speed. Smoked, it takes effect within minutes and lasts two to four hours; eaten, it can take more than an hour to kick in and last over six.

guide.text: Don't ride impaired by cannabis, legal or not: it skews your sense of time, distance and speed.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Fatigue.

content.question: Compared with driving a car, how quickly does riding a motorcycle tire you out?

choices.text: Faster, so you'll tire sooner on a long trip
About the same, over a trip of the same length
More slowly, since you're out in the fresh air
More slowly, as long as you are dressed warmly

content.explanation: A motorcycle asks more of your body than a car, so a long ride wears you down sooner than the same drive would. The weather adds to it: wind, cold and rain all drain you, which makes warm clothing and, for long trips, a windshield worthwhile.

guide.text: Riding wears you out sooner than driving, and wind, cold and rain speed that up, so dress for the weather.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Fatigue.

content.question: On a long ride, what is the best way to fight fatigue?

choices.text: Get off and rest at least every two hours
Take a stimulant once you begin to feel tired
Push on so the ride ends sooner
Open your visor for some fresh air

content.explanation: Tiredness costs you control, so build stops into a long ride and get off the motorcycle for a break no less often than every two hours. Stimulants are no fix: as they wear off they tend to leave you exhausted or low and unable to focus.

guide.text: Fight fatigue with real breaks, stopping to stretch your legs every two hours or sooner, not with stimulants.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Clothing.

content.question: It is cold and wet out. Why does it matter that your clothes keep you warm and dry?

choices.text: Getting cold makes the bike harder to control
It only matters for comfort, not for control
Being chilled keeps you more alert
Cold mainly affects the engine, not the rider

content.explanation: A rider who is chilled or numb from the cold handles the controls less precisely. Clothing that stays dry and a jacket that blocks the wind keep the cold from wearing you down on a long ride.

guide.text: Staying warm and dry matters for control: a chilled rider handles the motorcycle less well.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, under Get Familiar with the Controls.

content.question: You are about to ride a motorcycle you have never ridden before. Besides finding its controls, what should you do?

choices.text: Try each control a few times, then ride extra carefully
Ride it as you would your own, once it is checked
Trust your experience, since all controls work alike
Leave extra stopping room only if it is heavier

content.explanation: Get a feel for the levers, pedals and throttle while still parked, trying each a few times. Then treat the first miles as practice: leave more room to stop, take turns slower than usual and open the throttle gently.

guide.text: On a motorcycle new to you, try every control before setting off, then ride it gently until you know how it responds.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, under Check Your Motorcycle.

content.question: How often should you check your motorcycle before riding it?

choices.text: Before every ride
Before long trips only
Every few hundred miles
Only when something feels wrong

content.explanation: Make a quick inspection part of every ride, short trips included. Your owner's manual lists what to check and when the motorcycle is due for service.

guide.text: Inspect your motorcycle every time you ride, and follow the owner's manual for upkeep.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Tires and Wheels.

content.question: In a pre-ride check, you try each brake lever one at a time. What should you find?

choices.text: Both feel solid, and either one alone holds the motorcycle still
Each moves all the way to the grip without effort
Only the front needs to hold the motorcycle
A little sponginess, which is normal

content.explanation: Test the front and the rear separately. A good brake feels solid when you apply it fully and stops the motorcycle rolling on its own. Check at the same time that each one lights the brake light.

guide.text: Test each brake on its own: it should feel solid, hold the motorcycle still and light the brake light.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Controls.

content.question: In a pre-ride check, what should the throttle do when you release it?

choices.text: Snap back to fully closed
Stay where you left it until you close it
Return slowly, so the engine doesn't jerk
Hold a little open to keep the engine running

content.explanation: Try both controls before riding off. Let go of the throttle and it should spring all the way shut by itself, and the clutch should work smoothly with a tight feel.

guide.text: Before you ride, check that the throttle springs fully closed when released and that the clutch feels tight and smooth.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Lights and Electrics.

content.question: When should you adjust your motorcycle's mirrors?

choices.text: Before you start riding
At your first stop along the way
While rolling slowly through a parking lot
Once you are up to speed, to see real traffic

content.explanation: Each mirror should show the lane behind you and the lane alongside; a glimpse of your own arm at the edge doesn't matter. Get that set up before you move off, since fiddling with a mirror while riding means taking a hand off the bars.

guide.text: Set your mirrors before moving off, aimed at the lane behind you and the lane beside you.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Oil and Other Fluids.

content.question: How often should you check your brake hydraulic fluid and coolant, if your motorcycle has them?

choices.text: At least once a week
Only at each oil change
Once a year, at a service
Only when a warning light comes on

content.explanation: Brake fluid and coolant are weekly checks, if your motorcycle uses them. Oil and transmission levels belong in the check before each ride, along with a look at the ground under the motorcycle for drips.

guide.text: Weekly: brake fluid and coolant. Before every ride: oil and transmission levels, and a look underneath for leaks.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Oil and Other Fluids.

content.question: Your motorcycle has a fuel valve. Why make sure it is open before you leave?

choices.text: It can run briefly on the fuel already in the lines, then stall
The engine won't turn over at all with it closed
An open valve keeps fuel from leaking
It only matters on a cold morning

content.explanation: A closed valve doesn't stop the engine from starting: it can run for a short way on the fuel already in the lines. Once that runs out, the engine dies.

guide.text: Open the fuel valve, if there is one, before you ride. With it closed, a motorcycle can start, run briefly, then stall.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Stands.

content.question: In a pre-ride check, what should you make sure of with the side stand?

choices.text: Its spring keeps it firmly tucked up
It hangs loosely, ready to drop when you stop
It stays down until the engine has warmed up
It only needs checking if it has been bent

content.explanation: Flip the side stand down and back: it should move freely, and when raised its spring should keep it snug against the motorcycle. A center stand, if fitted, must also stay pulled up against the frame while you ride.

guide.text: Before riding, make sure the side stand moves freely and its spring keeps it firmly up, and that any center stand stays tucked against the frame.

meta.sourceSection: Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist, under Tires and Wheels.

content.question: When should you check your motorcycle's tire pressure?

choices.text: When the tires are cold
Right after a ride, while they are warm
Only when a tire looks low
Only before long trips

content.explanation: Check tire pressure when the tires are cold, and adjust it to the load you will carry.

guide.label: Tire pressure
guide.text: Check it with the tires cold, and adjust it to the load.

meta.sourceSection: Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist, under Controls.

content.question: With the engine idling, you turn the handlebars from side to side. What should the engine do?

choices.text: Keep idling steadily, without revving
Rev up slightly, which is normal
Drop its idle, then recover on its own
Rev a little, as long as the throttle snaps closed

content.explanation: The throttle should move freely and snap closed, and turning the handlebars should not make the engine rev. Cables should be routed so nothing pulls or catches at the steering head.

guide.text: With the engine idling, turning the handlebars from side to side should not make it rev.

meta.sourceSection: Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist, under Oil.

content.question: Which fluid should you check only when the engine is cool?

choices.text: Coolant
Engine oil
Brake fluid
Fuel

content.explanation: Check the coolant only when the engine is cool. Engine oil is the opposite: check it warm, with the motorcycle on its center stand on level ground.

guide.text: Check coolant only when cool. Check engine oil warm, on the center stand, on level ground.

meta.sourceSection: Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist, under Chassis.

content.question: Where along the drive chain should you check its tension?

choices.text: At its tightest point
At its loosest point
Right next to the rear sprocket
Anywhere, since it is the same all along

content.explanation: Measure chain slack at the tightest spot along it. Oil the side plates after a ride, while the chain is warm, and leave a belt drive dry.

guide.text: Measure chain slack at its tightest spot, oil the side plates while warm, and never oil a belt.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Quick Stops and Front-Wheel Skids.
meta.note: The manuals say to reapply firmly, smoothly, with less pressure, or with controlled gradual pressure. Firm but smooth, short of another lock, holds for every one of them.

content.question: Your front wheel locks in a hard stop, and you let go of the brake to get it rolling. How should you put the front brake back on?

choices.text: Firmly, but squeezed on smoothly so it does not lock again
With one quick, hard grab to win back the distance you lost
Barely at all, finishing the stop mostly on the rear brake
Not until the motorcycle is almost stopped, so it cannot lock twice

content.explanation: You still need the front brake to stop, so reapply it firmly, but squeeze it on smoothly. Grabbing at the front brake is what locks the wheel.

guide.text: After a front-wheel lock, reapply the front brake firmly but smoothly, never with a grab.

meta.sourceSection: Table 2A-1, sign shapes.

content.question: You can see an eight-sided sign ahead, but you are still too far away to read it. Which sign is it?

media.alt: A plain eight-sided outline with no color or lettering.

choices.text: A stop sign
A yield sign
A railroad crossing warning
A school zone warning

content.explanation: Only the stop sign may use the eight-sided shape, so its outline tells you to stop before you are close enough to read it.

guide.label: Octagon sign
guide.text: Stop. The shape is used for no other sign.

meta.sourceSection: Table 2A-1, sign shapes; Section 2B.05, YIELD signs.

content.question: What does a sign shaped like a downward-pointing triangle tell you to do?

media.alt: A plain triangle outline, pointing down, with no color or lettering.

choices.text: Slow, stop if needed, and let other traffic go first
Go ahead first, since cross traffic must wait for you
Give way to pedestrians, then go ahead of vehicles
Watch for a hazard ahead, then carry on at your speed

content.explanation: A triangle pointing down is reserved for the yield sign. Let other traffic go first, slowing or stopping if that is what it takes.

guide.label: Triangle sign, point down
guide.text: Yield. Let other traffic go first, slowing or stopping as needed.

meta.sourceSection: Table 2A-1, sign shapes; Section 8B.06, grade crossing advance warning.

content.question: What does a round sign beside the road warn you about?

media.alt: A plain circle outline with no color or lettering.

choices.text: A railroad crossing coming up
A traffic circle coming up
A stop sign coming up
A school crossing coming up

content.explanation: The circle is kept for one sign: the warning that a railroad crossing is coming up, posted on the road ahead of the tracks.

guide.label: Round sign
guide.text: A railroad crossing is ahead.

meta.sourceSection: Table 2A-1, sign shapes; Section 7B.02, school signs; Section 2C.02, colors.
meta.note: The MUTCD also gives the upward pentagon to county route markers, which have tapered lower sides, where the school sign's bottom corners are square.

content.question: A five-sided sign is shaped like the outline of a house, pointed at the top. What does it tell you?

media.alt: A plain five-sided outline shaped like a house, pointed at the top, with no color or lettering.

choices.text: A school zone or school crossing is near
A playground is beside the road
A railroad crossing is ahead
A hospital entrance is ahead

content.explanation: That outline belongs to the school sign, which marks a school area, the start of a school zone, or a crossing schoolchildren use. It is black on fluorescent yellow-green.

guide.label: Pentagon sign, point up
guide.text: A school area, school zone or school crossing.

meta.sourceSection: Table 2A-1, sign shapes; Section 2C.02, warning signs; Section 1C.02, definitions.

content.question: What kind of message does a diamond-shaped sign carry?

media.alt: A plain diamond outline with no color or lettering.

choices.text: A warning about something on the road ahead
A law you must obey, such as a speed limit
Directions, distances or the names of places
Services nearby, such as gas, food or lodging

content.explanation: Diamonds are warning signs. They point out something ahead that might not be obvious yet, such as a curve, a merge or a crossing.

guide.label: Diamond sign
guide.text: A warning about something ahead.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, under Shapes of Signs.

content.question: A rectangular sign is taller than it is wide. What kind of message does it usually carry?

media.alt: A plain rectangle outline, taller than it is wide, with no color or lettering.

choices.text: A rule you are required by law to follow
Directions, distances or the names of places
A warning about something on the road ahead
A non-binding suggestion you may choose to follow

content.explanation: Upright rectangles are usually regulatory signs, like a speed limit or a turn restriction, and each one states a rule you are required to follow.

guide.label: Upright rectangular sign
guide.text: Usually a regulation: a rule you are required to follow.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, under Shapes of Signs.

content.question: Which sign shape usually gives directions, distances or the names of places?

choices.text: A rectangle that is wider than it is tall
A rectangle that is taller than it is wide
A diamond standing on one of its points
A pentagon with its point at the top

content.explanation: A rectangle wider than it is tall is usually a guide sign, showing place names, route numbers, directions and distances.

guide.label: Wide rectangle
guide.text: Usually a guide sign: places, routes, directions and distances.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1D.05, color code; Sections 2B.02 and 2M.07, the red circle and diagonal.

content.question: A sign shows a picture inside a red circle, with a red line running diagonally across it. What does the sign tell you?

media.alt: A white sign with a black U-turn arrow, crossed by a red circle and a red diagonal line.

choices.text: What the picture shows is not allowed
What the picture shows is allowed here
What the picture shows is coming up ahead
What the picture shows ends at this point

content.explanation: The red circle and slash is the national symbol for a ban: whatever is pictured under the slash is not allowed.

guide.label: Sign with a red circle and slash
guide.text: Whatever is pictured inside is not allowed.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1D.05, color code; Section 2C.02, warning signs.

content.question: What does a yellow background usually tell you about a sign?

choices.text: It warns of something on the road ahead
It states a law you must obey
It marks a construction or work zone
It points the way to nearby services

content.explanation: In the national color code, yellow means warning, and most warning signs carry black lettering on yellow.

guide.label: Yellow sign
guide.text: Warning.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1D.05, color code; Section 6B.02, temporary traffic control zones.

content.question: What does an orange sign with black markings usually mean?

choices.text: A work zone or other temporary change to the road
A school zone, or a crossing used by schoolchildren
A permanent hazard, such as a sharp curve ahead
Gas, food or lodging available at the next exit

content.explanation: Orange marks temporary traffic control: work zones for construction, maintenance or utility work, and other short-term changes to the road.

guide.label: Orange sign
guide.text: Temporary traffic control, such as a work zone.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1D.05, color code; Section 2I.02, General Service signs.

content.question: A sign has white symbols and lettering on a blue background. What is it most likely telling you about?

choices.text: Services nearby, such as gas, food or a hospital
A regulation, such as a speed limit or turn rule
A hazard ahead, such as a curve or a dip
A temporary work zone on the road ahead

content.explanation: Blue is the color for road-user services, so a blue sign points you to things like gas, food, lodging, a hospital or camping.

guide.label: Blue sign
guide.text: Services, such as gas, food, lodging or a hospital.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2B.46, DO NOT ENTER sign.

content.question: A DO NOT ENTER sign faces you where a road begins. What does the sign tell you about that road?

media.alt: A red circle with a white bar across it and the words DO NOT ENTER.

choices.text: It carries one-way traffic coming at you
It is closed for road work ahead
It is a private road for residents only
It is a dead end with no way through

content.explanation: Every vehicle beyond this sign is headed your way. It is posted wherever a one-way road, a ramp or a divided-highway crossing could be entered against the flow.

guide.label: DO NOT ENTER
guide.text: Never ride past this sign, because the traffic beyond it is all one-way and headed at you.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2B.47, WRONG WAY sign; Section 2B.48, interchange ramps.

content.question: You have turned onto a ramp, and a red sign reading WRONG WAY now faces you. What does it mean?

media.alt: A red rectangular sign with white letters reading WRONG WAY.

choices.text: You are riding against the flow of traffic
You have missed your exit and should take the next
The ramp is closed ahead for road work
Your lane is ending, so merge with the next one

content.explanation: WRONG WAY signs stand along one-way roads and exit ramps, facing anyone headed the wrong direction. Seeing one means you are going against the traffic on it.

guide.label: WRONG WAY
guide.text: You are going against traffic on a one-way road or ramp.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2B.49, ONE WAY signs.
meta.note: The MUTCD's text does not say the arrow shows the permitted direction; the sign's figures, and its use to direct traffic around a roundabout, do.

content.question: At a corner, the street you want to turn onto has a ONE WAY sign whose arrow points to your right. Which way may you turn onto it?

media.alt: A black and white ONE WAY sign with its arrow pointing right.

choices.text: Right, the way the arrow points
Left, since the arrow shows oncoming traffic
Either way, if nothing is coming
Either way, keeping to the right-hand lane

content.explanation: Traffic on a ONE WAY street may travel in one direction only, and the sign's arrow shows which. Turn onto it the way the arrow points.

guide.label: ONE WAY
guide.text: Travel only the way the arrow points.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2B.60, No Turn on Red signs.
meta.note: The MUTCD states where an agency installs this sign, never what a rider must do, so the answer is the converse of an installation warrant.

content.question: You are stopped at a red light, waiting to turn right, and a sign by the signal reads NO TURN ON RED. Nothing is coming. What does the sign mean for you?

media.alt: A white rectangular sign with black letters reading NO TURN ON RED.

choices.text: You must wait for a signal that allows the turn
You may turn now that you have fully stopped
You may turn if you yield to people crossing
You may turn if the lane you enter is clear

content.explanation: The sign bans turning while the light is red. Even after a full stop with the way clear, you wait for a green light or a green arrow.

guide.label: NO TURN ON RED
guide.text: No turning while the light is red, even after a full stop.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.40, Reduced Speed Limit Ahead signs.

content.question: You pass a yellow diamond sign showing an upward arrow above a speed limit sign. Where does the lower limit take effect?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign showing a black arrow pointing up above a white sign reading SPEED LIMIT 55.

choices.text: At the speed limit sign posted farther along
Right here, at the sign you have just passed
Only where road conditions call for slowing
At the next intersection you come to

content.explanation: This sign gives advance notice. The lower limit begins at the speed limit sign that follows, so slow down in time to be at that speed when you reach it.

guide.label: Reduced speed limit ahead
guide.text: A lower limit starts at the speed limit sign ahead. Slow down in time.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7B.05, school speed limit signs; Section 4S.04, Speed Limit Sign Beacon.

content.question: A school speed limit sign has a pair of yellow lights and the words WHEN FLASHING. When does its lower limit apply?

choices.text: Only while the yellow lights are flashing
All day, on any day that school is open
Whenever children can be seen near the road
During school hours, whether or not the lights flash

content.explanation: The flashing lights mark the times the school limit is in force, so the lower limit applies while they flash.

guide.label: School limit WHEN FLASHING
guide.text: The lower limit applies while its yellow lights flash.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.59, Advisory Speed plaque; Section 1C.02, definitions.

content.question: Below a yellow curve warning sign is a small plaque showing a speed lower than the road's posted limit. What does that speed tell you?
