Give other vehicles extra room, especially as they pass or you pass them, and if the wind gets too strong to ride safely, stop somewhere safe until it eases.

guide.text: In a gust, push forward on the grip on the side the wind is coming from so the motorcycle leans into it. If it gets too strong, park until it eases.

meta.sourceSection: Section 9.1, Cold Weather.

content.question: You are riding on a cold day. Besides dressing warmly, how should you adjust your riding?

choices.text: Ride slower and leave more space ahead and beside you
Ride a little faster so you spend less time in the cold
Follow closer behind larger vehicles to stay out of the wind
Nothing changes, as long as your gear keeps you warm

content.explanation: Cold weather makes you slower to react. Give yourself the time back by easing your speed and leaving extra room in front and on both sides.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2.1, under Other Impairing Drugs and Riding.

content.question: Which drugs can affect your ability to ride safely?

choices.text: Illegal, prescribed and over-the-counter drugs alike
Only illegal drugs, since legal medicines are tested for safety
Only prescription drugs that carry a drowsiness warning
Only drugs taken together with alcohol

content.explanation: A medicine can impair your riding whether it came from a doctor, off a store shelf or from the street. When you're not sure about one, a doctor or pharmacist can tell you its side effects, and never combine any of them with alcohol, which they can make much stronger.

guide.text: Any drug, prescribed, bought over the counter or illegal, can impair your riding, and mixing one with alcohol makes it worse.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3.2, Getting to Know Your Motorcycle.

content.question: When should you set your mirrors, and what should they give you?

choices.text: Before you ride, set for the best view of the road behind
Once moving, when you can see how traffic is lined up behind
Only after a stop, when you notice a mirror has slipped
Before you ride, tilted down to show your rear wheel

content.explanation: Setting the mirrors is part of getting your motorcycle ready before you ride. Aim them for the best view of the road behind you.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3.3, Motorcycle Controls.

content.question: How well should you know your motorcycle's controls before you ride it?

choices.text: Well enough to use each one by feel, eyes on the road
Well enough to find each one with a quick glance down
The brakes and throttle only; the rest can wait until later
Well enough to name each one; using them comes with practice

content.explanation: Study the owner's manual until you can find and use every control by feel. On the road, your eyes belong on traffic.

guide.text: Learn every control from the owner's manual until you can use it by feel, without looking down.

meta.sourceSection: Section 4.3, Shifting Gears.

content.question: You want to change down to a lower gear. What do you do with the shift lever?

choices.text: Push it down with a firm but controlled foot
Lift it firmly, then let it spring back
Stamp down hard, so the gear is sure to engage
Press it down and keep holding it until you speed up

content.explanation: Close the throttle and pull in the clutch, then push the lever down with a deliberate, firm foot rather than a kick, and let it spring back. To go up a gear you lift it instead.

guide.text: Downshift by pushing the shift lever down and upshift by lifting it, using a firm foot but no stamping.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5.4, Space Management, under Lane Positions.

content.question: Big patches of oil and grease are a hazard to a motorcycle. Where do they usually build up?

choices.text: At busy intersections and toll booths
On the shoulders of rural highways
In the passing lane of an interstate
On bridge decks and overpasses

content.explanation: The thickest oil and grease deposits tend to be at busy intersections and toll booths, so steer around those patches.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.1, Crash Avoidance, under Stopping Quickly.

content.question: You need to stop as quickly as you can in a straight line. How should you brake?

choices.text: Both brakes together, pressed hard but stopping short of a skid
Downshift hard and let engine braking do the work
Pump the rear brake in quick bursts
Both brakes at full pressure from the very first instant

content.explanation: A motorcycle's shortest stop uses front and rear brakes together, pressed firmly but kept just below the point where either wheel would lock.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.1, Crash Avoidance, under Stopping Quickly.

content.question: During a quick stop, how should the pressure on your front brake change?

choices.text: Squeeze harder bit by bit as the front tire takes more weight
Start at full pressure, then ease off as you slow
Keep it steady from the first moment to the last
Ease it off as weight shifts forward, so the rear does more

content.explanation: As you brake, the motorcycle's weight moves forward onto the front tire, so increase front brake pressure gradually as the stop goes on instead of applying it all at the start.

guide.text: In a quick stop, squeeze the front brake harder by degrees as weight comes onto the front tire.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.1, Crash Avoidance, under Stopping Quickly.

content.question: During a quick stop, what posture helps keep the motorcycle stopping in a straight line?

choices.text: Gripping the tank with your knees, looking far down the road
Knees off the tank, eyes down on the front wheel
Leaning back with your arms locked straight
Knees relaxed, eyes on the pavement just ahead

content.explanation: In a quick stop, hold the tank between your knees and keep looking far down the road. That position keeps the motorcycle tracking straight while it stops.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.1, Crash Avoidance, under Anti-Lock Braking Systems (ABS).

content.question: Your motorcycle has anti-lock brakes, and you must stop quickly. What should you do?

choices.text: Brake hard with both brakes and keep holding, even if they pulse
Pump the brakes quickly, so the system has time to work
Use only the front brake; ABS makes the rear unnecessary
Ease off the moment you feel the brakes start to pulse

content.explanation: Anti-lock brakes let you use both brakes as hard as you need without locking a wheel. Squeeze and press firmly and keep the pressure on until you stop, even if the levers pulse. Most anti-lock systems are designed for braking upright and straight; leaned into a curve, a wheel may still lock.

guide.text: Anti-lock brakes: apply both brakes hard and keep holding, pulsing or not. Most can't prevent a lock-up while leaned over.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.1, Crash Avoidance, under Handling Skids.

content.question: Why must you release the front brake the instant the front wheel locks?

choices.text: With the front tire sliding, you can neither steer nor balance
To keep the front tire from wearing a flat spot
Because the engine stalls if the front wheel stops
Only on wet roads; on dry pavement you can hold the skid

content.explanation: The moment the front tire stops rolling, you can no longer steer or keep the motorcycle balanced. Let the lever go completely and right away, then reapply it gently. Hanging on to it ends in a fall.

guide.text: Front wheel locked: get off the front brake completely the instant it happens, then squeeze it back on gently. A sliding front tire can't steer or balance the motorcycle.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.3, Sharing the Road with Commercial Motor Vehicles.

content.question: While you pass another vehicle, what should you keep as short as possible?

choices.text: The time you spend in its blind spot
The space you leave before cutting back in front of it
How long your turn signal stays on before you move out
The gap between you and the vehicle as you go past

content.explanation: While you pass, get through the other vehicle's blind spot instead of riding along in it, since its driver cannot see you there.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7.4, Animals.

content.question: As you ride along, you spot a dog running toward the road to chase you. How should you handle it?

choices.text: Slow and drop a gear early, then accelerate away as it closes in
Speed up right away, before it can reach the road
Sound your horn and keep your speed steady
Keep your eyes on the dog and steer away from it

content.explanation: Ease off and select a lower gear while the dog is still on its way, then accelerate away firmly once it gets close. Look where you want to go rather than at the dog, and don't try to fend it off with your foot, which only upsets the motorcycle.

guide.text: When a dog gives chase, slow and gear down first, then pull away hard as it reaches you. Never kick at it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7.4, Animals.

content.question: A deer is standing near the edge of the road ahead of you. What should you do?

choices.text: Stop well before it, then wait or pass at a crawl
Sound your horn and speed past before it can move
Swerve wide around it while holding your speed
Slow slightly and pass, since deer run from traffic

content.explanation: Large animals such as deer move without warning, and striking one can do as much damage as striking a car. Brake to a stop before you get to it. Then either let it wander off or roll past slowly, no faster than a walk.

guide.text: A deer or other large animal on or beside the road: stop short of it, then wait or pass no faster than a walk.

meta.sourceSection: Section 8.1, Carrying Passengers and Cargo.

content.question: You are giving a small child a ride on your motorcycle. Where may the child sit?

choices.text: Behind you, the same as any other passenger
In front of you, where you can keep hold of them
In front, if they are small enough for you to see past
Wherever they feel safest, as long as they hold on

content.explanation: Every passenger, a child included, rides behind you, sitting close up rather than at the back of the seat.

meta.sourceSection: Section 8.1, Carrying Passengers and Cargo, under Instructing Passengers.

content.question: When should your passenger get on the motorcycle?

choices.text: Once the engine is already running
Before you start the engine, while the motorcycle is quiet
Whenever they are ready, since the timing does not matter
Once you have put it in gear and are ready to go

content.explanation: Start the engine first, and only then have your passenger climb on.

meta.sourceSection: Section 9.5, Fatigue.

content.question: You are setting out on a long ride on a cool, windy day. What will help keep fatigue down?

choices.text: Dress warm against the wind and cold, which drain your energy
Dress lightly, so the chill keeps you alert
Ride straight through, to finish before you tire
Take a stimulant to stay sharp for the whole ride

content.explanation: Riding exposed to wind, cold or rain uses up your energy fast, so warm clothing is part of staying alert. For long trips, a windshield helps for the same reason.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5.4, Space Management, under Following Another Vehicle.

content.question: In Georgia, a newer rider riding alone, not in a group, is advised to keep at least what gap behind the vehicle in front?

choices.text: At least four seconds
At least six seconds
At least eight seconds
At least one second

content.explanation: Georgia's manual recommends that newer riders leave at least four seconds to the vehicle in front when riding alone, which gives room to brake or steer around trouble. It asks for five or more at 40 mph and above, on slippery pavement, in heavy traffic, or behind a vehicle you can't see past.

guide.label: Following distance
guide.text: In Georgia, at least 4 seconds for a newer rider alone; 5 or more in poor conditions or at 40 mph and up.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5.4, Space Management, under Lane Positions.

content.question: Vehicles are moving in the lane to your right, and the lane to your left is empty. Where in your lane should you ride?

choices.text: The left or center portion, away from those vehicles
The right portion, so those drivers can see you clearly
The right portion, ready to move over if that lane frees up
Anywhere; only traffic in your own lane affects your position

content.explanation: Shift away from traffic beside you to keep a cushion of space. With vehicles on your right, ride in the left or center portion of your lane.

guide.text: Vehicles on your right only: ride the left or center of the lane.

meta.sourceSection: Preparing to Ride, Wear the Right Gear, under Helmet Use and Helmet Selection.

content.question: Under California law, who must wear a DOT-compliant motorcycle helmet?

choices.text: Every rider and every passenger
Riders only; passengers may choose
Riders and passengers under 21 only
Anyone riding on a freeway or highway

content.explanation: California requires every rider and every passenger to wear a helmet that meets the federal DOT standard. The DOT marking on the back should be the manufacturer's own, never a sticker. Eye and face protection is strongly advised but not required by law.

guide.text: In California, every rider and passenger must wear a DOT-compliant helmet carrying the maker's own DOT marking on the back, never a stick-on label. Eye protection is strongly advised, though the law doesn't require it.

meta.sourceSection: Preparing to Ride, Wear the Right Gear, under Face, Eye, and Ear Protection.

content.question: In California, may you ride with earplugs or earphones in both ears?

choices.text: Only hearing-protection earplugs that still let sirens and horns through
Yes, any earplugs or earphones, as long as the volume stays low
No, never; one ear must always stay uncovered while you ride
Yes, but only on freeways, where the wind noise is worst

content.explanation: California bars riding with both ears covered or plugged. Earplugs built as hearing protection are the exception, so long as sirens and other drivers' horns still come through.

guide.text: In California, nothing may cover or plug both ears while you ride, except hearing-protection earplugs that still let sirens and horns through.

meta.sourceSection: License Requirements, the M1/M2 requirements table, Note 4.

content.question: In California, what limits apply while you ride on a motorcycle instruction permit?

choices.text: No passengers, no freeways and no riding after dark
No passengers, but freeways and night riding are allowed
No freeways, but a licensed passenger may ride with you
No limits, as long as a licensed rider follows you

content.explanation: A California motorcycle permit bars three things: carrying a passenger, riding on a freeway and riding at night.

guide.label: California motorcycle permit limits
guide.text: No passengers, no freeways, no night riding.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Basic Vehicle Control, under U-turns.

content.question: You are making a slow, tight U-turn. Where should you keep the clutch for the most control?

choices.text: In the friction zone, where it is only partly engaged
Pulled fully in, so the motorcycle coasts through
Fully released, controlling speed with the throttle alone
Snapped in and out in quick bursts to keep speed down

content.explanation: Through a slow U-turn, keep the clutch in its friction zone, the band where it is only partly engaged, for the finest control of your speed.

guide.label: Friction zone
guide.text: The part of the clutch's travel where it is only partly engaged. Keeping it there gives the most control in a slow, tight turn.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Keeping Your Distance, under Carpool/HOV Lanes.

content.question: You are riding alone on a California freeway and want to use the carpool lane. Which is true?

choices.text: You may unless posted, entering only at marked openings
You may not, since a rider alone does not count as a carpool
You may, and you can cross its double lines wherever it is safe
You may, but you need a decal on the motorcycle to use it

content.explanation: A motorcycle may use a California carpool lane with only the rider aboard, unless signs say otherwise. Get in and out only at the marked entry and exit points, never across the double parallel lines.

guide.text: In California, motorcycles may use carpool lanes, a lone rider included, unless signs say otherwise. Enter and exit only at marked openings, never across the double lines.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Keeping Your Distance, under Following Another Vehicle.

content.question: Compared with a car in the same traffic, how much room does a motorcycle need to stop?

choices.text: About as much as the car needs
About half as much, since it weighs less
Twice as much, having only two tires
Less, as long as both brakes are used

content.explanation: A motorcycle needs roughly the same distance to stop as the cars around it, so leave yourself the same room ahead. Following too closely can contribute to a crash.

guide.label: A motorcycle's stopping distance
guide.text: About the same as other vehicles'.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Following Another Vehicle and Riding at Night.

content.question: In California, riding alone, not in a group, what is the minimum following distance you should normally keep behind the vehicle ahead?

choices.text: At least two seconds
At least one second
At least four seconds
At least five seconds

content.explanation: Two seconds is California's floor for normal riding, and even that leaves little margin if traffic ahead stops short. Stretch it to three seconds or more at night, in heavy traffic, on slippery pavement, or behind a vehicle that blocks your view ahead.

guide.label: California following distance
guide.text: At least 2 seconds normally; 3 or more at night or in poor conditions.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Laws and Rules of the Road, Sharing the Road, under Motorcycles.
meta.note: Only the Driver's Handbook states that lane splitting is legal; the Motorcycle Handbook defines it without saying so.

content.question: Traffic on a California freeway has slowed to a crawl in both lanes. May you ride between the two lanes of cars?

choices.text: Yes, lane splitting is legal in California
No, a motorcycle must stay within one lane
Not until the traffic has come to a full stop
Not unless a sign says lane splitting is allowed

content.explanation: Yes. Riding between lanes of cars, called lane splitting, is legal for motorcycles in California.

guide.text: In California, lane splitting, where a motorcycle rides between lanes of traffic, is legal.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Collision Avoidance.

content.question: Riders involved in collisions most often make which braking mistake?

choices.text: Too little front brake and too much rear
Too much front brake and too little rear
Using both brakes together instead of one
Braking too early, well before they need to

content.explanation: The usual braking error among riders in collisions is too much rear brake and too little front. The front supplies about three-quarters of your stopping power, so make full use of it, building pressure smoothly instead of grabbing the lever.

guide.text: In collisions, riders most often brake too hard at the rear and too lightly at the front.

meta.sourceSection: Carrying Passengers and Cargo, under Equipment.

content.question: You plan to carry a passenger. What should your motorcycle have first?

choices.text: A seat big enough for two, and footrests for the passenger
A backrest for the passenger, and a second pair of mirrors
Saddlebags for the passenger's gear, and a taller windshield
Handlebars moved so you can sit farther forward than usual

content.explanation: Before you take a passenger, check that the motorcycle has passenger footrests and a seat with room for both of you, so you can keep your usual riding position. The footrests matter for safety too, since a passenger with no solid footing can fall and drag you with them.

guide.text: To carry a passenger, have a seat with room for two and passenger footrests.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Blood Alcohol Concentration and Alcohol and the Law.

content.question: In California, at what blood alcohol concentration is it illegal to ride?

choices.text: 0.08 at 21 or older, 0.01 under 21
0.08 at 21 or older, 0.02 under 21
0.10 at 21 or older, 0.05 under 21
0.08 for every rider, whatever their age

content.explanation: California sets the limit at 0.08 for riders 21 and over and at 0.01 for anyone younger, its zero-tolerance level. How sober you seem makes no difference, since the legal question is settled by a breath or blood test.

guide.label: California BAC limit
guide.text: 0.08 at 21 or older; 0.01 under 21. A breath or blood test settles it, whatever your appearance.

meta.sourceSection: License Requirements, the M1 and M2 class list and the class chart.
meta.note: DL 665's class chart also lets any license class ride a short-term rental motorized bicycle, which is why the stem says the moped was bought.

content.question: You have bought a moped to ride in California. What is the lowest license class that lets you ride it?

choices.text: Class M2, which covers mopeds
Class M1, which covers motorcycles
Any class of driver's license
None, since a moped has pedals

content.explanation: In California a moped calls for at least a Class M2 license, which also covers motorized bicycles and scooters. A Class M1 covers every two-wheel motorcycle as well as everything an M2 does.

guide.label: California license classes
guide.text: M1: any two-wheel motorcycle, plus everything M2 covers. M2: mopeds, motorized bicycles and scooters only.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Eye and Face Protection.

content.question: Which of these must good eye or face protection do?

choices.text: Keep your view to both sides clear
Seal tightly, so no air reaches your eyes
Carry a tint, to cut glare day and night
Fasten loosely, so it flips up quickly

content.explanation: Eye or face protection has to leave your view to both sides clear. It should also let air through so it doesn't fog, stay free of scratches, resist punctures, leave room for glasses, and fasten firmly enough not to blow off.

guide.label: Eye protection
guide.text: Clear side vision, vented against fogging, scratch-free, puncture-resistant, room for glasses, fastened securely.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Basic Vehicle Control, under U-turns.

content.question: Which brake should you use to control your speed in a slow, tight U-turn?

choices.text: The rear brake, dragged lightly
The front brake, squeezed gently
Both brakes together, as for any stop
Neither, just the throttle and clutch

content.explanation: Leave the front brake alone in a tight, slow turn, since it can pull the motorcycle over. Your speed comes from a light, steady drag on the rear brake, which also steadies the motorcycle at a crawl.

guide.text: For speed control in a slow, tight U-turn, use a light drag on the rear brake and leave the front alone, since it can drop the motorcycle.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Lane Positions.

content.question: Which lane position is the best one for a motorcycle?

choices.text: It depends on traffic and road conditions
The left portion, next to the center line
The right portion, next to the curb
The center, away from both edges

content.explanation: No one spot in the lane is right all the time. The aim is to be visible with space on every side, and the place that does that moves as traffic and the road change.

guide.text: The best lane position is whichever one keeps you visible with space around you, and it changes as you ride.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Keeping Your Distance, under Passing.

content.question: You are passing a slower vehicle. May you go over the speed limit to finish the pass?

choices.text: No, a pass must be completed within the posted limit
Yes, briefly, to get back into your lane sooner
Yes, by up to 10 mph, as long as you are passing
Yes, on a two-lane road with little time to get by

content.explanation: No. The posted limit still applies while you pass, so if you can't get by without speeding, don't start. Pass only where it is allowed.

guide.text: Stay at or under the posted limit while passing, and pass only where it's allowed.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Increasing Visibility, under Turn Signals.

content.question: In California, how far ahead of a turn should you signal?

choices.text: Through the last 100 feet before the turn
Just as you start to make the turn
Through the last 25 feet before the turn
Only when another vehicle is close behind

content.explanation: Turn your signal on 100 feet before the corner and leave it on until you turn. A lane change at highway speed calls for more warning: five seconds or more. Signal every time, whether or not you see anyone around.

guide.label: California signal timing
guide.text: Turn: signal from 100 feet out. Highway lane change: 5 seconds or more.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Riding in a group, the first two riders make it through a green light before it turns red. What must the riders behind them do?

choices.text: Stop for the red light like any other vehicle
Follow through, so the group stays together
Follow through if the leader waves them on
Go through after a full stop, as a group

content.explanation: Group or not, each rider obeys stop signs and traffic lights on their own, just as any vehicle must. If the riders behind are stopped by a red light, those ahead ease off a little and let them catch up.

guide.text: In a group, every rider obeys signals and stop signs. Nobody runs a light to keep up.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6, Navigating the Roads, Turns; Section 7, Traffic Signals.

content.question: You are stopped at a red light and want to turn right. When may you make the turn?

choices.text: After a full stop, unless a sign forbids it or it is a red arrow
Without stopping, as long as no traffic is coming from the left
Only where a sign says turning right on red is allowed
Not until the light turns green, since red means stay stopped

content.explanation: Come to a full stop at the limit line, let pedestrians and cross traffic clear, and then the right turn is yours, provided no sign bans it. A red arrow is the exception and keeps you stopped until it turns green. Left on red is legal too, but only from one one-way street into another.

guide.label: Turning on red
guide.text: After a full stop, a right on red is legal unless a sign or a red arrow forbids it. A left on red is allowed only from one one-way street into another.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Laws and Rules of the Road, under Move Over and Slow Down.

content.question: In California, a tow truck is stopped on the shoulder ahead with its amber lights flashing. What does the law require of you?

choices.text: Move over and slow down as you go past
Nothing; a tow truck is not an emergency vehicle
Stop behind it until the driver waves you on
Slow down only if it blocks part of your lane

content.explanation: California's Move Over law reaches beyond police cars and ambulances. A tow truck stopped with amber lights flashing counts, and so does a road-work vehicle stopped with warning lights on, so move over and slow down as you go by.

guide.label: California's Move Over law
guide.text: Move over and slow down when passing a stopped emergency vehicle, tow truck or road-work vehicle that has its warning lights on.

meta.sourceSection: Section 8, Safe Driving, Understand the Road Conditions, under Darkness.

content.question: Riding at night, how should you set your speed?

choices.text: Slow enough to stop inside your headlight's reach
To match the speed of the traffic around you
To the posted limit, which already allows for darkness
So you can stop before the taillights you see ahead

content.explanation: After dark, never outride your headlight. If something appears at the edge of its beam, you need to be able to stop before you reach it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Laws and Rules of the Road, Sharing the Road, under Emergency Vehicles.

content.question: You are halfway across an intersection when an ambulance comes up behind you with its siren on and red lights flashing. What should you do?

choices.text: Keep going through, then pull to the right edge and stop
Stop right where you are, in the intersection
Speed up to stay well ahead of the ambulance
Move to the left so it can pass you on the right

content.explanation: Finish crossing the intersection first, then pull to the right edge and stop until the ambulance has gone by. Any emergency vehicle using its siren and red lights has the right-of-way, and once it passes, stay at least 300 feet behind it while the siren or lights stay on.

guide.label: Emergency vehicles
guide.text: Siren and red lights: pull over right and wait, finishing any intersection first. Then stay 300 feet or more behind it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Laws and Rules of the Road, under Around Children.

content.question: On a California road with one lane each way, a school bus stopped on the other side has its red lights flashing. What must you do?

choices.text: Stop, and stay stopped until the lights stop flashing
Slow down and pass with care, since it is across the road
Stop, then go once the children reach the curb
Nothing; only traffic behind the bus must stop

content.explanation: Traffic from both directions stays stopped while a school bus shows flashing red lights, and until the children are across. The only exception is a bus on the far side of a divided highway, or of a road with two or more lanes each way. Flashing yellow means the bus is about to stop, so ease off and get ready.

guide.label: California school bus lights
guide.text: Flashing red: both directions stop until the lights go off. Exception: the bus is across a divided road, or one with 2+ lanes each way. Flashing yellow: be ready to stop.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Laws and Rules of the Road, under Pedestrians.

content.question: The car in the lane beside you stops at a crosswalk, and you can't see why. What should you do?

choices.text: Stop as well; it may be hiding someone crossing
Ride on past, since your own lane is clear
Sound your horn, then pass it slowly
Pass it, as long as you see no one in the road

content.explanation: When a car has stopped at a crosswalk, someone may be crossing in front of it, hidden from your lane. Stop too, and don't go past it while it waits.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Laws and Rules of the Road, Right-of-Way Rules, under Intersections.

content.question: You and a car reach a four-way stop at the same moment, and the car is on your right. Who goes first?

choices.text: The car on your right
You, since the car is on your right
Whichever of you is going straight
The car, since it is the larger vehicle

content.explanation: When you both reach a four-way stop together, the vehicle on your right has priority, so let it go first. Otherwise, whoever got there first goes first, and the same order holds where there are no signs at all. Even when it's your turn, let the other driver go if insisting could cause a crash.

guide.label: All-way stops and uncontrolled intersections
guide.text: Whoever arrives first goes first. Arriving together, the vehicle on the right has priority. Yield anyway if insisting could cause a crash.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Laws and Rules of the Road, under Business or Residential Districts.

content.question: In California, what is the speed limit in a business or residential district when no limit is posted?

choices.text: 25 mph
30 mph
35 mph
20 mph

content.explanation: Unless signs say otherwise, a California business or residential district is 25 mph, and so is the zone within 500 feet of a school when children are outside or crossing. Alleys and blind intersections drop to 15 mph, as does the last 100 feet before a railroad crossing whose tracks you can't see for 400 feet both ways.

guide.label: California city speed limits
guide.text: 25 mph in business and residential districts and near a school with children outside; 15 mph in alleys and at blind intersections.

meta.sourceSection: Section 8, Safe Driving, under Manage Your Speed.

content.question: You are riding a divided California highway where no other limit is posted. What is the top speed?

choices.text: 65 mph
70 mph
55 mph
75 mph

content.explanation: California's default top speed is 65 mph on most highways, a divided one included, but 55 on a two-lane undivided highway. Posted signs override both, and the Basic Speed Law caps you lower still whenever conditions call for less.

guide.label: California highway speed limits
guide.text: 65 mph on most highways and 55 on two-lane undivided ones, unless posted. Never faster than conditions safely allow.

meta.sourceSection: Section 8, Safe Driving, under Cell Phones and Texting; Minors and Cell Phones.

content.question: Riding in California, how may an adult rider use a cell phone?

choices.text: Hands-free only, never holding it
Holding it for calls, but not for texting
Never; any cell phone use while operating a vehicle is always illegal
Texting is fine if the phone is mounted

content.explanation: The only legal way for an adult to use a phone while riding in California is hands-free, and only when needed. Holding the phone, or texting, is off limits, and riders under 18 can't use one at all, apart from calling for emergency help.

guide.text: In California, adults may ride with a phone only in hands-free mode, when necessary, and never to text. Riders under 18 may use one only to call for emergency help.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, An Introduction to Driving, under Using Your Headlights.

content.question: In California, you are riding at night with your high beam on. When must you switch to low beam?

choices.text: Within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle or 300 feet of one you follow
Within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle or 200 feet of one you follow
Within 1,000 feet of any vehicle, coming or going
Only when an oncoming driver flashes their lights at you

content.explanation: Switch to low beam once an oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet, or when you close to 300 feet behind the vehicle in front. With no one that close on a dark road, keep the high beam on.

guide.label: Dimming your high beam in California
guide.text: Within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle, and 300 feet of one you follow.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6, Navigating the Roads, under Crossing or Entering Traffic.

content.question: You are waiting to turn left, and an oncoming car has its right turn signal on. When is it safe to start your turn?

choices.text: Once the car actually begins its turn
As soon as you see its signal flashing
Once the car slows near the corner
When the driver waves you ahead

content.explanation: A turn signal on an oncoming car proves nothing until the car begins to turn. A signal left on by mistake looks just like a real one, and so does one meant for a turn past where you are waiting, so let the car commit before you start your own turn.

guide.text: Turning left across an oncoming car signaling right, wait until it actually starts to turn.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Laws and Rules of the Road, Sharing the Road, under Passing a Bicyclist.

content.question: In California, you come up behind a bicyclist in your lane and can't change lanes. Oncoming traffic leaves you only about two feet to pass. What should you do?

choices.text: Stay behind until you can give at least three feet
Pass slowly, using the two feet you have
Sound your horn so the rider moves over, then pass
Pass, as long as you keep under 15 mph

content.explanation: California requires a three-foot gap whenever you pass a bicyclist without changing lanes. With oncoming traffic leaving only two feet, the pass has to wait, so hold back behind the rider until you can give the full three.

guide.label: Passing a bicyclist in California
guide.text: At least 3 feet of clearance whenever you pass in the same lane, and no pass until you have it. A lane change gives more room still.

meta.sourceSection: Section 9, Alcohol and Drugs.

content.question: An over-the-counter allergy pill leaves you drowsy. Can riding after taking it count as DUI in California?

choices.text: Yes, if it affects your ability to ride safely
No, DUI covers only alcohol and illegal drugs
No, not for a medicine sold without a prescription
Only if you have also been drinking

content.explanation: Yes. California's DUI law reaches any medicine that impairs your riding, prescribed or bought off the shelf, just as it reaches alcohol and illegal drugs. Check the label, and find out how a new medicine affects you before you ride.

guide.text: In California, a medicine that impairs your riding can be DUI, prescribed or bought off the shelf.

meta.sourceSection: Section 9, Alcohol and Drugs, under DUI Arrests.

content.question: An officer suspects you of riding under the influence and asks you to take a chemical test. Which is true in California?

choices.text: By riding in California, you have already agreed to take it
You may refuse it with no effect on your license
You need take it only if you failed a roadside check
You may insist on a breath test and refuse blood or urine

content.explanation: California counts everyone using its roads as having agreed in advance to a chemical test when an officer suspects DUI: breath, blood or urine. Taking a breath test may not be the end of it; an officer checking for drugs can still require blood or urine.

guide.text: Using California's roads counts as agreeing in advance to a chemical test whenever an officer suspects DUI.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Laws and Rules of the Road, under Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks.

content.question: A train has just passed a crossing ahead, and the gate is rising, but the red lights are still flashing. What should you do?

choices.text: Stay stopped until the lights stop flashing
Go once the gate has gone all the way up
Go once you can see that the track is clear
Ride around the end of the gate as it rises

content.explanation: Wait for the red lights to go dark, even with the gate already rising, because a second train can be right behind the first on any track. Never weave around a lowered or lifting gate. While you wait, stay 15 feet or more back from the nearest rail, and when the lights stop, start across only if there is room to get completely clear on the far side.

guide.label: Railroad crossings
guide.text: Never go around a crossing gate, and wait for the flashing red lights to stop even after the gate lifts. Wait 15 feet or more back from the nearest rail, and only start across with room to clear the far side.

meta.sourceSection: Section 10, Collisions, under What to Do if You Are in a Collision.

content.question: You are in a minor crash, and no one is hurt. Which of these must you do?

choices.text: Show your license, registration and insurance to the other driver
Leave both vehicles exactly where they stopped until police arrive
Ride on, since no one was hurt and your motorcycle still runs
Report it to the police within one hour, even with no injuries

content.explanation: Leaving the scene of any crash is a hit-and-run, so stop. With nobody hurt, move the vehicles out of traffic and then call 911; if someone is hurt, call first. The other driver and the officer both get to see your license, registration and proof of insurance, along with your current address.

guide.label: After a crash
guide.text: Always stop. Someone hurt: call 911 first. No one hurt: clear the road, then call. Share license, registration, insurance and address.

meta.sourceSection: Motorcycle Insurance Facts.

content.question: In California, you are in a crash that causes a couple thousand dollars in damage but hurts no one. Must you report it to the DMV?

choices.text: Yes, within 10 days, though no one was hurt
No, the police report it to the DMV for you
No, only crashes with injuries are reported
Yes, but only if the crash was your fault

content.explanation: Yes. A crash that does more than $1,000 of damage needs your own report to the DMV within 10 days, and so does one that injures anyone at all. The police won't file it on your behalf.

guide.label: Reporting a crash in California
guide.text: Your own report to the DMV is due within 10 days of any crash with an injury or more than $1,000 in damage, and the police won't file it for you.

meta.sourceSection: Riding Texas Highways, under Helmet and Passengers.

content.question: Under Texas law, who may ride on a motorcycle without a helmet?

choices.text: Someone 21 or older who has completed an approved course or has medical insurance
Someone 18 or older who has completed an approved course or has medical insurance
Someone 21 or older, whether or not they have training or insurance
No one, since the law covers every rider and every passenger

content.explanation: Texas lets a rider or passenger leave the helmet off only after turning 21, and then only with either an approved training course behind them or medical insurance coverage. Everyone else must wear one that meets the federal standard, FMVSS 218. Even where the law allows it, going without gives up the best protection you have in a crash.

guide.text: In Texas, a helmet meeting FMVSS 218 is required unless the rider or passenger is 21 or older and has either finished an approved course or carries medical insurance.

meta.sourceSection: Riding Texas Highways, under Helmet and Passengers.

content.question: Under Texas law, what must a motorcycle have before it can carry a passenger?

choices.text: A permanent passenger seat, passenger footrests and handholds
Passenger footrests and a backrest the passenger can lean on
A passenger seat and a backrest, with footrests optional
Passenger footrests alone, on a seat with room for two

content.explanation: Texas requires a fixed passenger seat, passenger footrests and handholds before anyone rides behind you. The seat should also leave you room to sit where you normally do.

guide.text: In Texas, a passenger may ride only on a motorcycle with a fixed passenger seat, footrests for the passenger and handholds.

meta.sourceSection: Preparing to Ride, Know Your Motorcycle, under Borrowing and Lending.
meta.note: The manual's figure is under five months; six is deliberate, and holds for it too.

content.question: Which of these do more than half of all motorcycle crashes have in common?

choices.text: The rider has under six months of experience on their motorcycle
The rider ends up with a head or neck injury
The rider is over the legal alcohol limit
The crash comes late in a long trip, far from where it began

content.explanation: Riders with under six months on their motorcycle are in over half of all crashes. Even a veteran is back in that group on a new or borrowed bike, so ride it gently until you know how it handles.

guide.text: Riders in their first six months on a motorcycle are in over half of crashes. Take a new or borrowed bike gently.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Following Another Vehicle and Riding at Night.

content.question: Riding alone, not in a group, what minimum following distance does Texas expect you to keep behind the vehicle ahead in normal conditions?

choices.text: At least two seconds
At least one second
At least four seconds
At least five seconds

content.explanation: Two seconds is the least Texas wants you to leave in normal riding, a thin margin that barely covers braking or swerving if the vehicle ahead stops hard. Give yourself three seconds or more in heavy traffic, on slippery pavement, at night, or when you can't see past the vehicle ahead.

guide.label: Texas following distance
guide.text: At least 2 seconds; 3 or more at night, in heavy traffic or on slippery pavement.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Keeping Your Distance, under Passing.

content.question: You are passing a slower car. How fast does the law let you go to finish the pass?

choices.text: No faster than the posted speed limit
Up to 10 mph over the posted limit
As fast as it takes to finish quickly
Over the limit if the car speeds up too

content.explanation: Speeding to finish a pass is still speeding. Start one only where signs and pavement markings allow it, and only if you can get past without going over the posted limit.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Keeping Your Distance, under Lane Sharing.
meta.note: The manual calls lane sharing usually prohibited and never says illegal; the wording keeps to that.

content.question: In Texas, traffic ahead has stopped in both lanes at a red light. May you ride between the rows of cars to reach the front?

choices.text: No, stay in a full lane of your own
Yes, as long as the light stays red
Yes, if you go no faster than 10 mph
Yes, if you warn drivers with your horn

content.explanation: No. Texas's manual says lane sharing is generally prohibited and that a motorcycle needs a whole lane, just as a car does. Wedged between rows of traffic, stopped or rolling, you would have no escape from a door swinging open or a car changing lanes.

guide.text: Texas generally prohibits lane sharing, so hold a full lane of your own instead of riding between rows of cars.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Alcohol and the Law.

content.question: In Texas, at what blood alcohol concentration does riding become illegal?

choices.text: 0.08 at 21 or older; any detectable alcohol under 21
0.08 at 21 or older; a BAC of 0.02 or more under 21
0.10 at 21 or older; a BAC of 0.05 or more under 21
0.08 for every rider, no matter how old they are

content.explanation: Any measurable alcohol is an offense for a Texas rider under 21, under the state's zero-tolerance law. From 21 on, the line for legal intoxication is a BAC of 0.08, though your judgment and skills slip well before that.

guide.label: Texas BAC limit
guide.text: 0.08 at 21 or older; any detectable alcohol under 21.

meta.sourceSection: Florida-Specific Considerations, under Helmet Law.

content.question: Under Florida law, who may ride a motorcycle without a helmet?

choices.text: Someone over 21 insured for $10,000 or more in medical costs
Someone 18 or older insured for $10,000 or more in medical costs
Anyone over 21, whether or not they carry medical insurance
No one, since the law covers every rider and passenger

content.explanation: No Florida rider or passenger under 21 may go without a securely fastened, DOT-compliant helmet, whatever insurance they carry. Over 21, leaving it off is legal only with a policy covering $10,000 or more in crash-related medical costs.

guide.text: In Florida, riders and passengers under 21 must wear a DOT-compliant helmet. Over 21, it becomes optional only with insurance covering $10,000 or more in crash medical costs.

meta.sourceSection: Florida-Specific Considerations, under Eye Protection.
meta.note: Florida's handbook says eye protection is not required of passengers on one page and required of them on another, so the question asks about operators only.

content.question: Under Florida law, which motorcycle operators must wear approved eye protection?

choices.text: Every operator, with or without a helmet
Those riding without a helmet
Those whose motorcycle has no windshield
Those who are younger than 21

content.explanation: Florida requires approved eye protection, such as goggles or a face shield, on every motorcycle operator, including one legally riding without a helmet. A windshield is no substitute.

guide.text: In Florida, every motorcycle operator needs approved eye protection, with or without a helmet; a windshield doesn't qualify.

meta.sourceSection: Riding a Motorcycle in Florida, under Know Florida's Move Over Law.

content.question: On a Florida highway, a police car is stopped on the shoulder with its lights flashing, and traffic keeps you from moving over a lane. What must you do?

choices.text: Slow to 20 mph under the posted limit
Slow to 10 mph under the posted limit
Keep your speed, but ride the far side of your lane
Stop in your lane until you are able to move over

content.explanation: When you can't safely get out of the lane next to a stopped police car, Florida's Move Over law has you drop to 20 mph under the posted limit, or to 5 mph where the limit is 20 or lower. Changing lanes is the first choice whenever it is safe. The rule also covers disabled vehicles showing hazards or flares or with someone standing by, plus stopped road-work, utility, sanitation and tow vehicles with warning lights on.

guide.label: Florida's Move Over law
guide.text: Leave the lane beside a stopped emergency, tow, utility, road-work or disabled vehicle, or if you can't, ride 20 mph under the limit past it.

meta.sourceSection: Preparing to Ride, Know Your Motorcycle, under Get Familiar with the Motorcycle Controls.

content.question: On a motorcycle with a manual clutch, what is the friction zone?

choices.text: A short stretch of the clutch lever's movement that links engine to rear wheel
The first part of the throttle's turn, before the engine responds
The part of the brake lever's travel before the brake grips
The lever position with the clutch pulled all the way in

content.explanation: Between pulled in and fully released, the clutch lever passes through a narrow friction zone, which decides how much of the engine's power reaches the rear wheel. Know it well before you ride a motorcycle with a manual clutch.

guide.label: Friction zone
guide.text: The short band of clutch lever travel through which engine power is fed to the rear wheel.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Keeping Your Distance, under Passing.

content.question: Partway through passing a slow truck, you need more speed to get clear of it. What does the law allow?

choices.text: More speed, up to the posted speed limit
A brief burst over the limit to finish the pass
Up to 10 mph over the limit while you pass
Whatever speed gets the pass done safely

content.explanation: You may speed up to clear the truck, but only as far as the posted limit. Before starting any pass, check that signs and pavement markings permit one there.

guide.text: When passing, you may speed up only as far as the posted limit. Start a pass only where signs and pavement markings permit one.

meta.sourceSection: Florida-Specific Considerations, Rules of the Road, under Lane Splitting/Filtering.
meta.note: Florida's handbook uses "lane sharing" for riding between rows on one page and for two motorcycles abreast on another, so the wording keeps to lane splitting.

content.question: In Florida, highway traffic is creeping along in both lanes. May you ride between the two lines of cars to get ahead?

choices.text: No, Florida law keeps you within a lane
Yes, if traffic is moving under 30 mph
Yes, once traffic has come to a full stop
Yes, if you go no more than 10 mph faster

content.explanation: No. Whether traffic is crawling or stopped, a Florida rider must keep to one lane, and riding the gap between lanes, called lane splitting, is illegal. Between two lines of cars, a door that opens or a car that drifts over leaves you nowhere to go.

guide.text: In Florida a motorcycle keeps to a single lane, and lane splitting between rows of traffic is illegal even when it is stopped.

meta.sourceSection: Riding with Passengers or Cargo, under Equipment for Carrying a Passenger.

content.question: Under Florida law, what must a motorcycle have before it carries a passenger behind the rider?

choices.text: A seat that fits you both, and passenger footrests
Passenger footrests, and a backrest for the passenger
A seat that fits you both, and a passenger backrest
Saddlebags for the passenger's gear, and a second mirror

content.explanation: Florida law requires a seat roomy enough for two, so you keep your normal position, and passenger footrests unless the motorcycle has a sidecar or enclosed cab. Add a strap or handholds for the passenger to grip.

guide.text: In Florida, carrying a passenger requires passenger footrests and a seat big enough for two.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Alcohol and the Law.
meta.note: The handbook calls 0.08 DUI but ties 0.02 under 21 to a license suspension, so no field calls the under-21 figure DUI.

content.question: What blood alcohol limits does Florida set for riders?

choices.text: 0.08 at 21 or older; 0.02 under 21
0.08 at 21 or older; 0.04 under 21
0.10 at 21 or older; 0.02 under 21
0.08 for every rider, regardless of age

content.explanation: Florida's BAC limits are 0.08 at 21 and over and 0.02 under 21. Impaired faculties alone can make it DUI below 0.08, and a breath, blood or urine result outweighs how sober you look.

guide.label: Florida BAC limit
guide.text: 0.08 at 21 or older; 0.02 under 21. A breath, blood or urine test outweighs how sober you seem.

meta.sourceSection: Florida-Specific Considerations, under Motorcycle Equipment.

content.question: Under Florida law, how high may a motorcycle's handlebars be?

choices.text: No higher than the rider's shoulders
No higher than the top of the rider's head
No more than 15 inches above the seat
Any height the rider can reach comfortably

content.explanation: Handlebars in Florida may sit no higher than the rider's shoulders. Anything taller is a violation.

guide.label: Florida handlebar height
guide.text: No higher than the rider's shoulders.

meta.sourceSection: Florida-Specific Considerations, Rules of the Road, under Stuck on Red.

content.question: In Florida, a red light has not changed for a long time, and you suspect its sensor has missed your motorcycle. What should you do?

choices.text: Keep waiting, and move to where the sensor can find you
Treat it as a stop sign and go when the way is clear
Go through on red after waiting a full light cycle
Rev the engine so the sensor hears the motorcycle

content.explanation: Move the motorcycle to where the signal's pavement sensor is most sensitive. Many lights wait for a metal-sensing loop in the road to detect traffic, and a motorcycle off the loop's sweet spot can go unnoticed, while the loop's outline isn't always visible. Waiting it out is still the law, since Florida makes no exception for a red that seems stuck.

guide.text: In Florida, a red light that won't change still has to be obeyed. Position the motorcycle where the pavement sensor is most sensitive, even if you can't see the sensor.

meta.sourceSection: Appendix 3, Motorcycle Violations Checklist, item 27.
meta.note: The handbook's violations checklist lists wearing a headset not attached to the helmet and says no more, so the answer is that line's converse.

content.question: In Florida, may you ride wearing earbuds or headphones that are not part of your helmet?

choices.text: No, a headset must be attached to the helmet
Yes, as long as the volume stays low
Yes, if they are wireless instead of wired
Yes, but only on slower city streets

content.explanation: No. Florida counts riding with a headset that isn't attached to your helmet as a violation.

guide.text: In Florida, a headset must be attached to your helmet; riding with one that isn't is a violation.

content.question: How should a motorcycle helmet fit?

choices.text: Snugly, with no loose spots anywhere around your head
Loosely enough that it rocks a little from side to side
Snug at the forehead and loose at the back of the head
Loosely, since the fastened chin strap is what holds it on

content.explanation: Pick one that sits snug on every side of your head. A cracked shell, padding that has worked loose or frayed straps rule a helmet out, however well it fits.

guide.text: A helmet should fit snugly all round and be free of cracks, frayed straps and loose padding.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Clothing.

content.question: How should a riding jacket fit?

choices.text: Close enough that it won't flap, with room to move freely
Baggy, so air can flow through it on hot days
As tight as it will go, so nothing can snag on the motorcycle
Roomy, so it fits over whatever you wear underneath

content.explanation: A riding jacket that flaps in the wind is too loose, and one that limits your movement is too tight. Wear it with pants so your arms and legs are fully covered.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Clothing.

content.question: For protection in a crash, which riding jacket material is the best choice?

choices.text: Leather or a sturdy synthetic material
Heavy cotton, such as canvas or thick flannel
Wool, like the shell of a heavy winter coat
Whatever is brightest, since being seen counts most

content.explanation: For a riding jacket, leather and sturdy synthetic materials give the most protection if you go down.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Clothing.

content.question: What should your riding gloves be made of?

choices.text: Leather, or a material just as durable
Knit wool, which keeps your hands warm
Thin fabric, which lets you feel the controls
Thin latex, which grips well in the rain

content.explanation: Leather, or another material that tough, is what riding gloves should be made of. A good pair protects your hands and improves your grip on the controls.

guide.text: Riding gloves should be leather or another equally durable material.

content.question: Riding a quiet rural road, you pass this sign. What does it warn you of?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign with a black arrow that bends to the right at a right angle.

choices.text: A sharp turn to the right ahead
A gentle curve to the right ahead
A side road joining from the right
A right turn required at the next road

content.explanation: The arrow's right-angle bend marks a sharp turn to the right. A gentler bend gets the curve sign, whose arrow bends gradually.

guide.label: Turn sign
guide.text: A sharp turn ahead, in the direction the arrow bends.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.07, horizontal alignment signs; Figure 2C-1.

content.question: Leaving town on a state highway, you pass this sign. What lies ahead?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign with a black arrow that snakes upward through several bends.

choices.text: Several bends close together ahead
One sharp bend ahead
A slippery stretch of road ahead
The road narrows ahead

content.explanation: The winding road sign warns of three or more bends close together ahead.

guide.label: Winding road sign
guide.text: Three or more bends close together ahead.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.41, intersection warning signs; Figure 2C-10.

content.question: This sign appears beside the highway ahead of you. What is it telling you?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign with a black vertical line and a shorter line meeting it from the right.

choices.text: A side road joins from the right ahead
Another road crosses yours ahead
Traffic merges in from the right ahead
Your road ends ahead at a crossing road

content.explanation: This sign warns that a side road enters from the right ahead, so watch for vehicles turning into or out of it.

guide.label: Side road sign
guide.text: A road joins from the side shown. Watch for traffic turning in or out.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.41, intersection warning signs; Figure 2C-10.

content.question: Riding a quiet county road, you come to this sign. What does it tell you?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign with a black symbol shaped like a capital T.

choices.text: Your road ends ahead, so you must turn
Another road crosses yours ahead
A side road joins from the left or right
The road narrows to a single lane

content.explanation: The T-intersection sign warns that the road you are on ends ahead at a crossing road, so you will have to turn one way or the other.

guide.label: T-intersection sign
guide.text: Your road ends ahead at a crossing road, and you will have to turn.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.21, Divided Highway Ends sign; Figure 2C-6.

content.question: This sign stands beside the highway you are on. What change does it warn of?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign showing a black island at the bottom center, with a downward arrow on its left and an upward arrow on its right that curve in toward each other above it.

choices.text: The median ends, and two-way traffic begins
A median begins, splitting the two directions
Keep to the right of an island ahead
The road gets narrower ahead

content.explanation: This sign warns that the divided highway ends ahead. The median stops, and from there traffic in both directions shares one road.

guide.label: Divided highway ends sign
guide.text: The median stops ahead, and two-way traffic begins.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.51, Two-Way Traffic sign; Figure 2C-11.

content.question: What should you be ready for after passing this sign?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign with two black arrows side by side, one pointing up and one pointing down.

choices.text: Traffic moving both ways on the road ahead
Traffic may pass on either side of an island
A divided highway with a median begins
Traffic merging in from both sides

content.explanation: The two-way traffic sign warns that you are moving onto a road where traffic runs in both directions, often after a one-way or divided stretch.

guide.label: Two-way traffic sign
guide.text: Traffic in both directions ahead, often after a divided or one-way stretch.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.35, advance traffic control signs; Figure 2C-8.

content.question: This sign comes up before a sharp bend on a back road. What does it tell you?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign showing a small red eight-sided shape with a black arrow above it, pointing up.

choices.text: A stop sign is ahead, so begin slowing
Stop right here, at this sign
A yield sign is ahead, so be ready to yield
A traffic signal is ahead

content.explanation: This sign warns of a stop sign ahead that you may not see in time, often because of a curve or a hill. Begin slowing for it.

guide.label: Stop ahead sign
guide.text: A stop sign is coming up that you may not see yet. Start slowing.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.35, advance traffic control signs; Figure 2C-8.

content.question: Coming over the top of a rise, you see this sign. What is ahead?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign showing a traffic light with red, yellow and green lenses.

choices.text: A traffic signal is ahead
A railroad crossing with lights is ahead
A school zone with flashing lights is ahead
A stop sign is ahead

content.explanation: This sign warns of a traffic signal ahead, posted where you might not see the signal in time to react to it.

guide.label: Signal ahead sign
guide.text: A traffic signal is coming up that you may not see yet.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.45, Merge signs; Figure 2C-11.

content.question: Riding in the right lane of a highway, you pass this sign. What should you be ready for?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign with a black upward arrow and a curved line joining it from the lower right.

choices.text: Traffic from another road joins yours from the right
Your lane ends ahead, so you must move left
A new lane is added on the right ahead
A side road crosses yours from the right

content.explanation: The merge sign warns that traffic from another road will merge into yours from the side shown. A lane that ends gets a different sign.

guide.label: Merge sign
guide.text: Traffic from another road joins yours from the side shown.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.47, Lane Ends signs; Figure 2C-11.

content.question: You are riding in the right-hand lane of a multi-lane road and see this sign. What does it mean for you?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign showing a solid black line on the left and, on the right, a line that angles in toward it partway up, with a short dashed line between them below the angle.

choices.text: Your lane ends ahead, so you must merge left
Traffic will merge into yours from the right
The road bends gently to the left ahead
A left-turn lane opens up ahead

content.explanation: This sign warns that the number of lanes drops ahead. If yours is the lane that ends, you have to merge into the lane beside it.

guide.label: Lane ends sign
guide.text: A lane ends ahead. Traffic in it must merge into the next lane.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.30, surface condition signs; Figure 2C-7.

content.question: You see this sign on a road you are riding for the first time. What should you know about the road ahead?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign showing a black car with two wavy lines trailing behind it.

choices.text: It can be slippery when wet
It has several bends close together
It has loose gravel on it
It has a rough, broken surface

content.explanation: This sign warns of a stretch of road that can be unexpectedly slippery when it is wet.

guide.label: Slippery when wet sign
guide.text: The road ahead can be slippery when wet.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.14, Hill signs; Figure 2C-5.

content.question: Riding along a rural highway, you pass this sign. What is it warning you about?

media.alt: A yellow diamond sign showing a black truck on a slope that drops to the right.

choices.text: A steep downhill grade ahead
Trucks crossing the road ahead
A runaway truck ramp ahead
A lane for slow trucks ahead

content.explanation: The hill sign warns of a downgrade long or steep enough to call for special care on the way down.

guide.label: Hill sign
guide.text: A steep or long downgrade ahead.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2B.39, Keep Right and Keep Left signs; Figure 2B-10.

content.question: This sign stands at the near end of a raised island in the middle of the road. What does it tell you?

media.alt: A white upright rectangular sign showing a black arrow that curves up past the right side of a black shield-shaped island.

choices.text: Pass the island only on its right side
Pass the island only on its left side
Pass on either side of the island
Stop and yield before passing the island

content.explanation: The keep right sign means traffic must pass only to the right of the island or obstruction it stands on.

guide.label: Keep right sign
guide.text: Pass only to the right of the island or obstruction.
